Cardiac fibroma.description: A benign primary cardiac tumor composed of dense collagen and fibroblasts, most often arising intramurally in the ventricular wall (especially the left ventricle).

Left ventricular thrombus.description: An intraventricular blood clot often forming along akinetic/dyskinetic endocardial surfaces after infarction or with severe cardiomyopathy.

Cardiac myxoma.description: The most common benign cardiac tumor, usually arising from the left atrial septum as a pedunculated, gelatinous mass that can be mobile and embolize.

Cardiac rhabdomyoma.description: A benign hamartomatous tumor of cardiac muscle, most common in infants and associated with tuberous sclerosis; often multiple intramyocardial nodules.

Primary cardiac sarcoma (e.g., fibrosarc.description: A rare malignant cardiac tumor that is infiltrative, often rapidly enlarging, with heterogeneous enhancement, necrosis, and histologic atypia.

Thoracic paraspinal neuroblastoma (dumbb.description: A malignant tumor of sympathetic nervous system origin, often arising from paraspinal sympathetic chain in children; may extend through the neural foramen into the spinal canal (dumbbell configuration) and shows internal vascularity and heterogeneous enhancement.

Ganglioneuroblastoma / Ganglioneuroma (n.description: Neoplasms along the spectrum from malignant (ganglioneuroblastoma) to benign (ganglioneuroma) arising from sympathetic chain; commonly paraspinal, may form dumbbell masses and enhance variably.

Nerve sheath tumor (schwannoma or neurof.normalized_text: Nerve sheath tumor (schwannoma or neurofibroma) with dumbbell extension
Nerve sheath tumor (schwannoma or neurof.description: Benign tumors arising from intercostal or spinal nerve roots; can extend through the neural foramen, forming a dumbbell shape, and often enhance on MRI.

Paraspinal abscess (epidural/paraspinal).description: Infectious collection adjacent to the spine that may extend into the epidural space; typically shows rim enhancement and peripheral hyperemia with systemic signs of infection.

Extramedullary hematopoiesis (paraspinal.description: Benign proliferation of hematopoietic tissue occurring outside the marrow, often presenting as bilateral paraspinal masses in patients with chronic anemia or hemoglobinopathies.

Simple hepatic cyst.description: A benign, congenital fluid-filled cavity in the liver, typically asymptomatic and discovered incidentally on imaging.

Hepatic hydatid (echinococcal) cyst.description: Parasitic infection by Echinococcus leading to cyst formation in the liver; may show daughter cysts, septations, or calcifications.

Pyogenic liver abscess.description: A bacterial infection resulting in a pus-filled cavity in the liver; often presents with fever, right upper quadrant pain, and elevated inflammatory markers.

Cystic hepatic metastasis.description: Secondary liver tumors from primaries such as mucinous gastrointestinal cancers or ovarian tumors that can appear cystic or necrotic on imaging.

Biliary cystic neoplasm (biliary cystade.description: A rare cystic tumor of the intrahepatic bile ducts that may be multilocular with septations and has malignant potential (cystadenocarcinoma).

Primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG).description: A chronic, progressive optic neuropathy characterized by retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) loss and corresponding visual field defects, often associated with elevated or fluctuating intraocular pressure but sometimes occurring with normal pressures.

Multiple sclerosis with prior optic neur.normalized_text: Multiple sclerosis with prior optic neuritis
Multiple sclerosis with prior optic neur.description: An inflammatory demyelinating disease of the central nervous system; optic neuritis is a frequent manifestation and can leave residual RNFL thinning, especially temporally, after the acute episode resolves.

Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (.normalized_text: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD)–related optic neuritis
Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (.description: An autoimmune astrocytopathy targeting AQP4, often causing severe, bilateral optic neuritis with marked RNFL thinning and longitudinally extensive spinal cord lesions.

Non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic ne.description: An ischemic infarct of the anterior optic nerve head, usually in older patients, leading to altitudinal visual field loss and segmental RNFL thinning after the acute swelling resolves.

Compressive optic neuropathy (e.g., chia.normalized_text: Compressive optic neuropathy (e.g., chiasmal or orbital compression)
Compressive optic neuropathy (e.g., chia.description: Damage to the optic nerve or chiasm from compressive lesions (pituitary adenoma, meningioma, orbital masses) leading to chronic RNFL thinning, often with temporal pallor and bitemporal field defects when chiasmal.

Bệnh Wilson (thoái hóa gan gan).description: Một rối loạn vận chuyển đồng lặn trên nhiễm sắc thể thường do đột biến ATP7B gây ra suy giảm bài tiết và tích tụ đồng mật ở gan, não (hạch nền) và giác mạc.

Thoái hóa thần kinh kèm theo tích tụ sắt.normalized_text: Thoái hóa thần kinh kèm theo tích tụ sắt trong não (ví dụ: PKAN)
Thoái hóa thần kinh kèm theo tích tụ sắt.description: Một nhóm các rối loạn di truyền, đặc trưng bởi sự tích tụ sắt quá mức ở hạch đáy gây rối loạn vận động và các thay đổi đặc trưng trên MRI.

Lắng đọng mangan do bệnh gan mãn tính (m.normalized_text: Lắng đọng mangan do bệnh gan mãn tính (mangan liên quan đến bệnh não gan)
Lắng đọng mangan do bệnh gan mãn tính (m.description: Ở rối loạn gan giai đoạn nặng, sự suy giảm khả năng loại bỏ mangan có thể gây tăng cường độ T1 ở hạch nền và các triệu chứng ngoài hình chóp.

Bệnh gan tắc mật mạn tính với tích tụ đồ.normalized_text: Bệnh gan tắc mật mạn tính với tích tụ đồng thứ phát (ví dụ: viêm đường mật nguyên phát hoặc tắc mật kéo dài)
Bệnh gan tắc mật mạn tính với tích tụ đồ.description: Lưu lượng mật giảm có thể gây giữ đồng thứ phát trong gan và đôi khi gây lắng đọng đồng ở giác mạc.

Phổ aceruloplasminemia/hemochromatosis (.normalized_text: Phổ aceruloplasminemia/hemochromatosis (rối loạn quá tải sắt toàn thân)
Phổ aceruloplasminemia/hemochromatosis (.description: Rối loạn chuyển hóa sắt di truyền dẫn đến sự lắng đỡ sắt ở nhiều cơ quan, bao gồm cả hạch nền, với các kết quả MRI đặc trưng.

Prepatellar bursitis (aseptic).description: Inflammation of the prepatellar bursa, often from repetitive kneeling or minor trauma, causing anterior knee swelling and localized tenderness; may have mild overlying erythema.

Septic prepatellar bursitis.description: Infection of the prepatellar bursa (commonly Staphylococcus aureus), presenting with anterior knee swelling, warmth, erythema, and tenderness; may have fever and systemic symptoms.

Cellulitis of the knee region.description: Bacterial infection of the skin and subcutaneous tissues causing diffuse redness, warmth, swelling, and tenderness; often spreads beyond a focal structure.

Septic arthritis of the knee.description: Infection within the knee joint causing an acutely swollen, painful, and warm joint; typically with marked limitation of motion and systemic illness.

Gout (acute gouty arthritis of the knee).normalized_text: Gout (acute gouty arthritis of the knee)
Gout (acute gouty arthritis of the knee).description: Inflammatory arthritis due to monosodium urate crystal deposition; presents with acute onset of a red, hot, swollen joint; knees can be involved though first MTP is most common.

Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease.description: Acute inflammatory arthritis due to calcium pyrophosphate crystals; often affects larger joints like the knee and mimics gout or septic arthritis.

Retropharyngeal abscess.description: A deep neck space infection located in the retropharyngeal space that can contain pus and gas, potentially life‑threatening due to airway compromise and mediastinal spread.

Cervical esophageal perforation.description: A tear or rupture of the cervical esophagus leading to extraluminal air and potential infection in the retropharyngeal or prevertebral spaces.

Ingested fish bone impaction (hypopharyn.normalized_text: Ingested fish bone impaction (hypopharynx/cervical esophagus) with secondary soft‑tissue emphysema
Ingested fish bone impaction (hypopharyn.description: A sharp, radiopaque foreign body (often fish bone) lodged in the hypopharynx or upper esophagus that can cause local perforation and introduce air into deep neck spaces.

Necrotizing soft tissue infection of the.normalized_text: Necrotizing soft tissue infection of the neck (necrotizing fasciitis)
Necrotizing soft tissue infection of the.description: A rapidly progressive infection causing soft‑tissue necrosis, often with gas formation in fascial planes; can arise from pharyngeal or dental sources and spread along deep neck spaces.

Traumatic laryngeal/hypopharyngeal injur.description: Disruption of laryngeal or hypopharyngeal structures due to trauma (including iatrogenic injury) that can introduce air into adjacent spaces and cause swelling.

Insulinoma (pancreatic beta-cell tumor).description: A neuroendocrine tumor of pancreatic beta cells causing autonomous insulin secretion and recurrent fasting hypoglycemia.

Sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia (facti.description: Hypoglycemia due to ingestion of insulin secretagogues (e.g., sulfonylureas) that stimulate endogenous insulin release.

Noninsulinoma pancreatogenous hypoglycem.description: Diffuse beta-cell hyperfunction (often post–bariatric surgery) causing inappropriate insulin secretion and fasting or postprandial hypoglycemia.

Insulin autoimmune syndrome (Hirata dise.description: Autoantibodies bind endogenous insulin, causing episodes of hypoglycemia with elevated total insulin; often triggered by certain drugs or occurring in predisposed individuals.

Exogenous insulin administration (factit.description: Use of injected insulin leading to hypoglycemia; typically associated with high insulin levels and suppressed ketogenesis.

Nutritional rickets (vitamin D deficienc.description: Metabolic bone disease in children caused by inadequate vitamin D leading to defective mineralization of the growth plate and bone, often producing a rachitic rosary (beading of costochondral junctions).

Renal osteodystrophy with secondary hype.normalized_text: Renal osteodystrophy with secondary hyperparathyroidism (calcipenic rickets)
Renal osteodystrophy with secondary hype.description: Bone changes from chronic kidney disease and secondary hyperparathyroidism causing defective mineralization and rickets-like changes in growing children.

Phosphate-wasting rickets (e.g., X-linke.description: Inherited or acquired renal phosphate loss causing hypophosphatemia, impaired mineralization, and rickets in children.

Scurvy (vitamin C deficiency) with scorb.normalized_text: Scurvy (vitamin C deficiency) with scorbutic rosary
Scurvy (vitamin C deficiency) with scorb.description: Deficiency of vitamin C leading to impaired collagen synthesis; in children can cause a scorbutic rosary (prominence at costochondral junctions) though typically sharper and with adjacent depression.

Tietze syndrome (localized costochondral.description: Benign, self-limited inflammation of a single costochondral junction, usually in the upper ribs, causing localized swelling and pain.

Pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis (PCI).description: Presence of multiple gas-filled cysts within the submucosa or subserosa of the bowel wall; often benign/idiopathic or secondary to other gastrointestinal or pulmonary conditions.

Colitis cystica profunda.description: Benign condition characterized by mucin-filled cysts in the submucosa due to mucosal herniation, often in the rectum; can mimic neoplasm endoscopically.

Colonic lymphangioma/lymphangiomatosis.description: Benign vascular malformation of lymphatic channels forming submucosal cystic lesions; can present as multiple translucent polypoid masses.

Ischemic colitis.description: Transient or persistent colonic ischemia causing mucosal edema, hemorrhage, and possible ulceration; commonly presents with abdominal pain and hematochezia.

Emphysematous colitis (infectious/necrot.normalized_text: Emphysematous colitis (infectious/necrotizing colitis with intramural gas)
Emphysematous colitis (infectious/necrot.description: Severe, often life-threatening colitis due to gas-forming organisms leading to intramural gas with systemic toxicity.

Leucemia eosinofílica crónica, NOS (CEL-.description: Una neoplasia mieloide clonal caracterizada por hipereosinofilia persistente con evidencia de clonalidad mieloide y ausencia de PDGFRA/PDGFRB/FGFR1 u otros reordenamientos definitorios.

Síndrome mielodisplásico con eosinofilia.description: Un trastorno clonal de la médula ósea con displasia y citopenias; algunos casos presentan eosinofilia periférica y anomalías citogenéticas como pérdida o ganancia de 1q.

Neoplasia mieloide/linfoide con eosinofi.normalized_text: Neoplasia mieloide/linfoide con eosinofilia y reorganización de tirosina quinasa (por ejemplo, PDGFRA/PDGFRB/FGFR1)
Neoplasia mieloide/linfoide con eosinofi.description: Neoplasias mieloides impulsadas por fusión que presentan hipereosinofilia; a menudo responden a inhibidores de tirosina quinasa dependiendo de la reorganización.

Síndrome idiopático hipereosinofílico (H.normalized_text: Síndrome idiopático hipereosinofílico (HES), posible variante linfocítica
Síndrome idiopático hipereosinofílico (H.description: Un trastorno con eosinofilia sostenida (>1500/μL) que causa afectación de órganos; la variante linfocítica está impulsada por células T productoras de IL-5 y a menudo muestra IgE elevada y receptores solubles de IL-2.

Infección parasitaria helmintica (por ej.normalized_text: Infección parasitaria helmintica (por ejemplo, strongiloidiasis o anquilostomícola)
Infección parasitaria helmintica (por ej.description: Las infecciones parasitarias suelen causar eosinofilia; el anquilostomas puede causar anemia por pérdida de sangre, y algunos helmintos elevan la IgE.

Anemia megaloblástica debida a deficienc.normalized_text: Anemia megaloblástica debida a deficiencia de vitamina B12 o folato
Anemia megaloblástica debida a deficienc.description: Deficiencia de vitamina B12 o folato que causa hematopoyesis ineficaz, macrocitosis, neutrófilos hipersegmentados y anemia.

diagnoses.name: Mixed-cellularity subtype of classic Hodgkin's lymphoma
diagnoses.normalized_text: Mixed-cellularity subtype of classic Hodgkin's lymphoma

Rosai–Dorfman disease (sinus histiocytos.normalized_text: Rosai–Dorfman disease (sinus histiocytosis with massive lymphadenopathy) with gastrointestinal involvement
Rosai–Dorfman disease (sinus histiocytos.description: A benign histiocytic proliferative disorder characterized by S100+/CD68+ histiocytes showing emperipolesis and typically CD1a negative; can present with nodal and extranodal disease, including bowel lesions that can act as a lead point for intussusception.

Burkitt lymphoma (intestinal/ileocecal).description: An aggressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma commonly involving the ileocecal region in children; rapidly growing mass can cause intussusception and marked FDG avidity.

Langerhans cell histiocytosis (gastroint.description: Clonal proliferation of Langerhans cells that can involve the GI tract; lesions may be FDG-avid and produce masses or strictures that could precipitate intussusception.

Meckel’s diverticulum or enteric duplica.normalized_text: Meckel’s diverticulum or enteric duplication cyst acting as a lead point
Meckel’s diverticulum or enteric duplica.description: Congenital anomalies of the distal ileum that can act as a lead point for ileo-ileal or ileocecal intussusception in children.

Inflammatory fibroid polyp (Vanek tumor).normalized_text: Inflammatory fibroid polyp (Vanek tumor) of the ileum/ileocecum
Inflammatory fibroid polyp (Vanek tumor).description: A rare benign submucosal lesion composed of spindle cells and eosinophils that can occur in the small bowel and act as a lead point for intussusception.

Severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria.description: A life-threatening parasitic infection of red blood cells that can cause hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, hepatic dysfunction, and acute kidney injury; confirmed by rapid diagnostic test and peripheral smear with ring forms.

Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP.description: A thrombotic microangiopathy due to ADAMTS13 deficiency causing platelet consumption and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with possible neurologic and renal involvement.

Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS).description: A thrombotic microangiopathy often triggered by Shiga-toxin–producing organisms leading to hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury.

Dengue with plasma leak (hemorrhagic/den.description: A viral infection causing capillary leak and thrombocytopenia; can present with hemoconcentration, transaminitis, and hyponatremia.

Babesiosis.description: A tick-borne intraerythrocytic parasitic infection causing hemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia, clinically similar to malaria.

Sepsis with disseminated intravascular c.description: A systemic inflammatory response to infection causing coagulopathy, platelet consumption, organ dysfunction, and potential hemolysis.

Cervical esophageal perforation with med.description: A tear of the cervical esophagus, often due to instrumentation or procedures, leading to leakage of secretions/contrast and secondary infection of the mediastinum.

Boerhaave syndrome (spontaneous esophage.description: Full-thickness esophageal rupture typically after forceful emesis, causing mediastinal contamination and severe infection.

Hypopharyngeal (pyriform sinus) perforat.normalized_text: Hypopharyngeal (pyriform sinus) perforation with descending mediastinitis
Hypopharyngeal (pyriform sinus) perforat.description: A perforation of the hypopharynx (e.g., pyriform sinus) that allows oropharyngeal secretions to track into the mediastinum, causing infection.

Esophageal perforation due to foreign bo.normalized_text: Esophageal perforation due to foreign body
Esophageal perforation due to foreign bo.description: A sharp or impacted foreign body causes a transmural tear of the esophagus, leading to leakage and mediastinitis.

Zenker’s diverticulum complicated by per.description: A pharyngoesophageal diverticulum arising above the upper esophageal sphincter that can rarely perforate or leak, leading to infection.

Complicated parapneumonic effusion (empy.description: Infected pleural fluid collection that often follows bacterial pneumonia; characterized by loculated pleural fluid, pleural thickening/enhancement, and adjacent lung consolidation.

Hydropneumothorax due to bronchopleural.description: Simultaneous pleural air and fluid caused by a communication between the bronchial tree and pleural space; may occur after necrotizing pneumonia, ruptured lung abscess, or surgery/trauma.

Lung abscess with parapneumonic effusion.description: Localized necrotizing infection of lung parenchyma causing a cavity with an air-fluid level; often communicates with bronchi and may cause an associated reactive or infected pleural effusion.

Malignant pleural effusion with trapped.normalized_text: Malignant pleural effusion with trapped lung
Malignant pleural effusion with trapped.description: Pleural fluid accumulation caused by pleural metastasis or mesothelioma; can lead to a nonexpanding lung and pleural thickening.

Tuberculous pleurisy with secondary empy.normalized_text: Tuberculous pleurisy with secondary empyema (possibly with bronchopleural fistula)
Tuberculous pleurisy with secondary empy.description: Mycobacterial infection involving the pleura causing exudative effusion that can become chronic and infected; chronic cases may form empyema and fistulae with pleural air.

Lennox-Gastaut syndrome (LGS).description: A severe developmental epileptic encephalopathy characterized by multiple seizure types, cognitive/behavioral impairment, and a characteristic EEG with generalized slow spike-and-wave (~1.5–2.5 Hz) and paroxysmal fast activity.

Childhood absence epilepsy (CAE).description: An idiopathic generalized epilepsy presenting in school-age children with brief staring spells and a classic EEG pattern of generalized 3-Hz spike-and-wave bursts.

Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME).description: A common idiopathic generalized epilepsy with myoclonic jerks, often on awakening, and EEG showing generalized 4–6 Hz polyspike-and-wave discharges.

Absence status epilepticus (nonconvulsiv.normalized_text: Absence status epilepticus (nonconvulsive status epilepticus of generalized onset)
Absence status epilepticus (nonconvulsiv.description: Prolonged or repeated absence activity leading to continuous or near-continuous impaired responsiveness with generalized spike-and-wave on EEG.

Meckel's diverticulitis (± small-bowel o.description: Inflammation of a congenital true diverticulum arising from the antimesenteric border of the distal ileum; can mimic appendicitis and may cause obstruction from inflammation, volvulus around a fibrous band, or intussusception.

Acute appendicitis.description: Inflammation of the vermiform appendix, typically arising from the cecal base; presents with right lower quadrant pain and can have a blind-ending inflamed tubular structure on imaging.

Jejunoileal (non-Meckel) small-bowel div.description: Inflammation of acquired small-bowel diverticula, usually on the mesenteric border and often multiple; can cause localized inflammatory changes and, less commonly, obstruction or perforation.

Terminal ileitis from Crohn's disease.description: Chronic transmural inflammatory bowel disease commonly involving the terminal ileum; can present with segmental ileitis, strictures, and obstruction.

Small-bowel obstruction due to adhesive.normalized_text: Small-bowel obstruction due to adhesive band or other mechanical cause (non-diverticular)
Small-bowel obstruction due to adhesive.description: Mechanical obstruction of the small intestine, commonly from postoperative adhesions, hernias, or masses; presents with dilated proximal loops and a transition point.

Susac syndrome (retinocochleocerebral va.description: An autoimmune microangiopathy that causes branch retinal artery occlusions (BRAOs), encephalopathy with characteristic corpus callosum lesions, and sensorineural hearing loss.

Primary angiitis of the central nervous.normalized_text: Primary angiitis of the central nervous system (PACNS) with ocular involvement
Primary angiitis of the central nervous.description: Inflammation of small- to medium-sized cerebral vessels that can cause multifocal brain ischemia and, less commonly, retinal arterial occlusions; may also affect the inner ear vasculature.

Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome (APS).description: A hypercoagulable disorder that causes arterial and venous thrombosis, which can involve retinal arteries and cerebral circulation; inner ear ischemia can lead to sensorineural hearing loss.

Multiple sclerosis (MS) with coincident.normalized_text: Multiple sclerosis (MS) with coincident retinal ischemia
Multiple sclerosis (MS) with coincident.description: A demyelinating disease of the CNS that can produce callosal lesions and visual field defects from optic pathway involvement; retinal ischemia would be atypical but possible if coexisting vascular event occurs.

Embolic branch retinal artery occlusion.normalized_text: Embolic branch retinal artery occlusion with unrelated sensorineural hearing loss
Embolic branch retinal artery occlusion.description: A focal retinal ischemic event from emboli (e.g., carotid or cardiac) causing sectoral retinal whitening and corresponding visual field loss; hearing loss could be due to another otologic cause.

Mitochondrial myopathy (e.g., MERRF spec.normalized_text: Mitochondrial myopathy (e.g., MERRF spectrum or mitochondrial cytopathy)
Mitochondrial myopathy (e.g., MERRF spec.description: A group of disorders caused by defects in mitochondrial DNA or nuclear genes affecting oxidative phosphorylation; classically shows ragged‑red fibers and COX‑negative fibers with multisystem involvement such as myopathy and seizures.

Myofibrillar myopathy (DES gene–related,.description: An autosomal dominant myopathy characterized by aggregation of desmin and other proteins leading to progressive muscle weakness, often with early axial/paraspinal involvement causing camptocormia; CK can be mildly to moderately elevated.

Facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (.description: A common autosomal dominant muscular dystrophy due to D4Z4 repeat contraction or SMCHD1 variants; presents with slowly progressive weakness that often involves facial, scapular, and truncal muscles and can include paraspinal weakness with camptocormia.

Late-onset Pompe disease (acid α‑glucosi.description: An autosomal recessive metabolic myopathy causing glycogen accumulation; presents with proximal and axial weakness, paraspinal involvement leading to bent spine, and respiratory muscle weakness; CK can be elevated.

diagnoses.normalized_text: B-cell lymphoma, unclassifiable, with features intermediate between diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and Burkitt lymphoma
diagnoses.icd11_title: B-cell lymphoma unclassifiable with features intermediate between Burkitt lymphoma and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

Burkitt lymphoma/leukemia (mature B‑cell.normalized_text: Burkitt lymphoma/leukemia (mature B‑cell neoplasm with MYC rearrangement)
Burkitt lymphoma/leukemia (mature B‑cell.description: Aggressive mature B‑cell lymphoma often presenting with bone marrow and blood involvement; characterized by MYC translocation, extremely high proliferation, and monomorphic medium-sized cells.

High‑grade B‑cell lymphoma with MYC and.normalized_text: High‑grade B‑cell lymphoma with MYC and BCL2 and/or BCL6 rearrangements (double‑/triple‑hit lymphoma)
High‑grade B‑cell lymphoma with MYC and.description: A very aggressive lymphoma showing MYC plus BCL2 and/or BCL6 rearrangements; overlaps morphologically with Burkitt and diffuse large B‑cell lymphoma and often presents with high tumor burden and marrow involvement.

Diffuse large B‑cell lymphoma (DLBCL), g.normalized_text: Diffuse large B‑cell lymphoma (DLBCL), germinal‑center B‑cell type
Diffuse large B‑cell lymphoma (DLBCL), g.description: The most common aggressive B‑cell lymphoma; GCB subtype often expresses CD10/BCL6 and has high proliferation; may secondarily acquire MYC rearrangements but not obligatory.

B‑lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma (B‑ALL.description: Neoplasm of precursor B‑cells typically TdT positive; presents with marrow blasts and high proliferation; cytogenetics vary and may show complex abnormalities but do not require MYC/IGH.

Pyogenic liver abscess.description: Bacterial infection of the liver resulting in one or more pus-filled cavities, often arising from biliary tract infection, portal seeding, or hematogenous spread.

Amoebic liver abscess.description: Hepatic abscess caused by Entamoeba histolytica; usually solitary and in the right lobe but may be multiple, especially in some presentations.

Hepatic metastases.description: Secondary malignant tumors of the liver from a primary cancer elsewhere; commonly present as multiple hypovascular or hypervascular lesions depending on primary.

Hepatic hemangiomas (multiple).description: Benign vascular tumors of the liver; can be multiple; typically show peripheral nodular enhancement with progressive fill-in on contrast imaging.

Hepatic involvement by lymphoma.description: Primary or secondary hepatic lymphoma presenting with diffuse infiltration or multiple hypodense lesions, often with hepatomegaly and sometimes splenomegaly.

Hepatic hydatid disease (echinococcosis).description: Parasitic infection by Echinococcus leading to cystic hepatic lesions which may show daughter cysts, calcifications, or heterogeneous contents if complicated.

diagnoses.name: ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction
diagnoses.icd11_title: Acute ST segment elevation myocardial infarction

Acute anterior wall STEMI (LAD occlusion.description: Transmural myocardial infarction due to occlusion of the left anterior descending artery, producing localized ischemia/injury in the anterior-septal/lateral walls.

Hyperkalemia (early ECG manifestations).description: Elevated serum potassium causes characteristic ECG changes progressing from peaked T waves to conduction widening and arrhythmias.

Benign early repolarization.description: A non-ischemic variant with J-point elevation and concave ST elevation, often seen in young/healthy individuals.

Acute pericarditis.description: Inflammation of the pericardium causing diffuse ST elevation and PR-segment depression.

Coronary vasospasm (Prinzmetal/variant a.description: Transient focal coronary artery spasm causing episodic transmural ischemia with temporary ST elevation.

Pulmonary sequestration (congenital syst.description: A congenital, nonfunctioning segment of lung that lacks normal bronchial communication and receives arterial blood supply from the systemic circulation (usually the aorta). Can present in neonates with respiratory distress and a posterior basal mass; may be intralobar or extralobar.

Congenital pulmonary airway malformation.description: A developmental cystic lung lesion composed of abnormal communicating airways; may present as a cystic or solid mass and cause respiratory distress in neonates.

Congenital diaphragmatic hernia (Bochdal.description: A defect in the posterolateral diaphragm allowing abdominal contents to herniate into the thorax, causing pulmonary hypoplasia and respiratory distress.

Neonatal pneumothorax.description: Air in the pleural space in a newborn, often presenting with acute respiratory distress and unilateral hyperlucency on chest radiograph.

Lobar overinflation (congenital lobar em.description: Overexpansion of a lung lobe due to intrinsic or extrinsic bronchial obstruction, leading to respiratory distress in neonates.

Neonatal pneumonia/atelectasis (focal).description: Infection or collapse of a lung segment/lobe causing focal opacification and respiratory distress in a newborn.

Malignant hypertension with hyperplastic.description: Severe, accelerated hypertension causing concentric smooth muscle and basement membrane proliferation in small arteries/arterioles (onion-skin lesions) leading to luminal narrowing and ischemic injury.

Scleroderma renal crisis.description: A microvascular complication of systemic sclerosis characterized by abrupt severe hypertension and TMA-like vascular lesions, including onion-skin arteriolar changes and intimal proliferation.

Thrombotic microangiopathy (e.g., TTP/HU.description: TMA encompasses disorders with endothelial injury leading to arteriolar/arterial intimal proliferation, basement membrane duplication, and possible thrombi; can be due to TTP, HUS, drugs, infections, or complement dysregulation.

Chronic allograft vasculopathy / transpl.description: Chronic antibody-mediated injury in renal allografts producing intimal fibroplasia of arteries and multilayering/duplication of basement membranes (double-contours), sometimes with onion-skin arteriolar changes.

Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome–assoc.description: A prothrombotic autoimmune condition causing renal vascular lesions including TMA-like changes, fibrous intimal hyperplasia, and onion-skin arteriolar lesions.

Chiari I malformation.description: Congenital condition characterized by herniation of the cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum due to a small posterior fossa, causing crowding at the craniocervical junction and potential brainstem/medullary compression.

Chiari 1.5 malformation.description: Variant of Chiari I in which there is descent not only of the cerebellar tonsils but also of the brainstem and obex, leading to more pronounced cervicomedullary crowding and symptoms.

Basilar invagination (craniovertebral ju.description: Congenital or acquired upward displacement of the odontoid into the foramen magnum that can compress the medulla and cerebellar tonsils, mimicking or coexisting with Chiari-type crowding.

Acquired tonsillar herniation from poste.normalized_text: Acquired tonsillar herniation from posterior fossa mass effect
Acquired tonsillar herniation from poste.description: Space-occupying lesion in the posterior fossa (e.g., tumor, cyst) can cause crowding and downward displacement of the cerebellar tonsils, leading to obstructed CSF flow and brainstem compression.

Spontaneous intracranial hypotension wit.normalized_text: Spontaneous intracranial hypotension with brain sag
Spontaneous intracranial hypotension wit.description: Low CSF pressure from spinal CSF leak causes brain sagging and secondary tonsillar descent that can resemble Chiari I on imaging, often with orthostatic symptoms and pachymeningeal enhancement.

Enterokokk (ehtimol vankomisinga chidaml.normalized_text: Enterokokk (ehtimol vankomisinga chidamli Enterokok) sababli yuqumli endokardit
Enterokokk (ehtimol vankomisinga chidaml.description: Endokardial yuza, ko'pincha klapanlar, Enterococcus spp. tomonidan infeksiyalanadi. Enterokoklar sefalosporinlarga tabiiy ravishda chidamli; ba'zi shtammlar (masalan, E. faecium yoki E. gallinarum/casseliflavus) vankomisinga chidamli bo'lishi mumkin, ammo penitsillin/ampitsillinga nisbatan sezgir bo'lib qoladi. Katta o'simliklar va aortaning qaytishi yuzaga kelishi mumkin.

Staphylococcus aureus infektiv endokardi.description: Yurak klapanlarining agressiv bakterial infeksiyasi odatda S. aureus tomonidan yuzaga keladi, ko'pincha katta, mo'rin o'simliklarni yuzaga keltiradi va klapan keskin buzilishi natijasida qaytish holatiga olib keladi.

Qo'ziqorin (Candida) endokarditi.description: Candida spp. tomonidan yuzaga keladigan endokardit, ko'pincha katta o'simliklar, oldingi antibiotiklar, IV kateterlar yoki protez klapanlar bilan bog'liq bo'lib, og'ir qaytish va embolik hodisalarga olib kelishi mumkin.

Bakterial bo'lmagan trombotik endokardit.description: Valflarda steril fibrin-trombotsit o'simliklari, ko'pincha o'sma yoki tizimli yallig'lanish bilan bog'liq; qaytish va emboliya keltirib chiqarishi mumkin, lekin yuqumli organizmlar yo'q.

Pulmonary embolism with pulmonary infarc.description: Acute thromboembolus lodged in a segmental/subsegmental pulmonary artery causing ischemia and a pleural-based wedge-shaped pulmonary infarct.

Community-acquired pneumonia (focal peri.description: Infectious consolidation of lung parenchyma that can appear as a peripheral, wedge-like opacity, especially with pleuritic involvement.

Septic pulmonary emboli.description: Embolization of infected thrombi (often from right-sided endocarditis or thrombophlebitis) leading to peripheral nodules/infarcts that may be wedge-shaped and pleural-based.

Pulmonary infarct from nonthrombotic emb.normalized_text: Pulmonary infarct from nonthrombotic emboli (e.g., fat, tumor, air)
Pulmonary infarct from nonthrombotic emb.description: Nonthrombotic material lodging in distal pulmonary arteries causing ischemic, pleural-based infarcts that can mimic thromboembolic PE on imaging.

Peripheral pulmonary neoplasm (e.g., ade.normalized_text: Peripheral pulmonary neoplasm (e.g., adenocarcinoma) with post-obstructive change
Peripheral pulmonary neoplasm (e.g., ade.description: A peripheral lung mass or nodule can appear near the pleura and may be associated with localized atelectasis or consolidation that can look wedge-like.

Herpes simplex virus (HSV) encephalitis.description: Acute necrotizing encephalitis, most often due to HSV-1, with predilection for the mesial temporal lobes and insula causing rapidly progressive encephalopathy and seizures.

Autoimmune/paraneoplastic limbic encepha.description: Immune-mediated inflammation of the limbic system (often associated with antibodies such as LGI1, CASPR2, NMDA-R, Hu), presenting with subacute memory impairment, behavioral change, and seizures.

Postictal changes/status epilepticus-rel.description: Transient MRI changes after prolonged seizures/status epilepticus due to cytotoxic/vasogenic edema, often involving mesial temporal structures, cortex, and hippocampus.

Low-grade glioma (e.g., diffuse astrocyt.normalized_text: Low-grade glioma (e.g., diffuse astrocytoma) in the temporal lobe
Low-grade glioma (e.g., diffuse astrocyt.description: Infiltrative primary brain tumor that can present with seizures and T2/FLAIR hyperintensity with minimal enhancement, often without marked mass effect early.

Subacute ischemic infarct of the tempora.normalized_text: Subacute ischemic infarct of the temporal lobe (MCA territory) or hippocampal stroke
Subacute ischemic infarct of the tempora.description: Ischemia/infarction involving temporal cortex or hippocampus can cause T2/FLAIR hyperintensity and sometimes transient enhancement in the subacute phase.

Severe bacterial pneumonia with sepsis a.normalized_text: Severe bacterial pneumonia with sepsis and ARDS
Severe bacterial pneumonia with sepsis a.description: A severe lung infection leading to systemic inflammatory response and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), characterized by shunt physiology, hypoxemia refractory to oxygen, and multiorgan stress.

Rhabdomyolysis.description: Skeletal muscle breakdown releasing intracellular contents (CK, potassium, myoglobin) leading to electrolyte disturbances and risk of acute kidney injury.

Type 2 myocardial infarction (demand isc.normalized_text: Type 2 myocardial infarction (demand ischemia) or acute myocardial injury
Type 2 myocardial infarction (demand isc.description: Myocardial injury from supply–demand mismatch due to severe systemic illness (hypoxia, sepsis, respiratory failure), resulting in elevated cardiac biomarkers without primary coronary plaque rupture.

Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH).description: A hyperinflammatory syndrome characterized by excessive immune activation leading to high ferritin, elevated soluble IL-2 receptor, liver enzyme elevations, and often cytopenias; can be triggered by infection.

Ischemic hepatitis (shock liver) seconda.normalized_text: Ischemic hepatitis (shock liver) secondary to hypoxia/shock
Ischemic hepatitis (shock liver) seconda.description: Hepatocellular injury from reduced perfusion/oxygenation during shock or severe hypoxemia, causing transaminase and LDH elevations.

Tumorframkallað osteomalasi (fosfaturur.normalized_text: Tumorframkallað osteomalasi (fosfaturur mesenchymal tumor, sum seytir FGF23)
Tumorframkallað osteomalasi (fosfaturur.description: Eitt paraneoplastiskt syndrom orsakað av FGF23-útskrivandi tumorum, sum elva til nyrnafosfat-burturkast, lágt/vanligt kalsium, hægri alkalisk fosfatasa orsakað av osteomalacia, óhóskandi høgt ella vanligt 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, og hægri FGF23. Burturtøka av tumorinum rættar biokemiskar óreglur.

X-bundin hypofosfatemi (XLH).description: Ein arvaligur FGF23-miðlaður nýrnafosfat-útslát orsakað av PHEX-mutatiónum; vísir seg í barnalagnum við kroniskari hypofosfatemi, hækkaðum FGF23, lágum/vanligum 1,25D, og osteomalasiu/rickets.

Primær hyperparathyroidismi.description: Sjálvstøðug PTH-útskiljing (ofta frá parathyroid adenoma) elvir til hyperkalsemiu og burturkast av nýrnafosfati, við hægri PTH og øktari beinskifti.

Fanconi syndrom (proximal renal tubular.description: Ein almennur proximal tubular defektur, sum førir til fosfat í urini og aðrar leystar evni, sum elvir til hypofosfatemi og osteomalasiu.

Arvaligur hypofosfatemiskur rakiti við h.description: Ein autosomal víkjandi sjúka (SLC34A3 mutatiónir), sum elvir til nýrafosfat við lágum FGF23, høgum 1,25D, hyperkalciuriu og raket/osteomalasiu.

Left-sided infective endocarditis (likel.normalized_text: Left-sided infective endocarditis (likely aortic valve) with systemic embolization
Left-sided infective endocarditis (likel.description: Infection of the cardiac endocardium, most often involving the aortic or mitral valve, producing friable vegetations that can embolize to the brain and spleen and may cause valvular destruction with aortic regurgitation.

Nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis (ma.description: Sterile fibrin-platelet vegetations on cardiac valves, often associated with malignancy or a hypercoagulable state, that can embolize systemically.

Cardiac myxoma with embolic phenomena.description: Benign intracardiac tumor (usually left atrial) that can fragment and embolize to the brain and systemic circulation.

Atrial fibrillation with left atrial/app.normalized_text: Atrial fibrillation with left atrial/appendage thrombus causing cardioembolic events
Atrial fibrillation with left atrial/app.description: Thrombus formation in the left atrium or appendage due to atrial fibrillation leading to systemic embolization to the brain and spleen.

Libman–Sacks endocarditis (SLE/antiphosp.description: Sterile verrucous vegetations on valves associated with systemic lupus erythematosus or antiphospholipid syndrome that can embolize.

Cranioectodermal dysplasia (Sensenbrenne.description: A ciliopathy characterized by craniosynostosis/dolichocephaly, ectodermal defects (sparse hair, small teeth, nail dystrophy), skeletal dysplasia with narrow chest and limb shortening, and nephronophthisis leading to progressive renal failure; ocular issues and recurrent respiratory infections are common.

Mainzer–Saldino syndrome (Short-rib thor.normalized_text: Mainzer–Saldino syndrome (Short-rib thoracic dysplasia type 10, often due to IFT140)
Mainzer–Saldino syndrome (Short-rib thor.description: A ciliopathy combining nephronophthisis-driven renal failure, skeletal dysplasia (epiphyseal/ metaphyseal changes, brachydactyly, short ribs/narrow thorax), and retinal/ocular disease; growth and neurodevelopment can be normal.

Jeune asphyxiating thoracic dystrophy (S.normalized_text: Jeune asphyxiating thoracic dystrophy (Short-rib thoracic dysplasia)
Jeune asphyxiating thoracic dystrophy (S.description: A short-rib thoracic dysplasia characterized by a narrow, bell-shaped thorax and short ribs with variable limb shortening; some patients develop renal and ocular involvement. Respiratory issues and recurrent infections are common in early childhood.

Nail–patella syndrome (LMX1B-related).description: An autosomal dominant disorder featuring hypoplastic/dysplastic nails, musculoskeletal anomalies (patella, elbows, iliac horns), and kidney disease (often proteinuric glomerulopathy) with variable ocular involvement.

Lowe syndrome (oculocerebrorenal syndrom.description: A disorder with congenital ocular abnormalities (notably cataracts), proximal renal tubular dysfunction leading to renal failure, and neurologic involvement with hypotonia and developmental delay.

Acrokeratosis paraneoplastica (Bazex syn.description: A paraneoplastic dermatosis presenting with psoriasiform, violaceous, scaly plaques on acral sites (hands, feet, ears, nose) and nail dystrophy, most often associated with squamous cell carcinomas of the upper aerodigestive tract or esophagus. Cutaneous findings often precede cancer diagnosis.

Dermatomyositis (paraneoplastic variant.description: An autoimmune inflammatory myopathy characterized by cutaneous findings (Gottron papules/sign on dorsal MCP/PIP joints, heliotrope rash) and proximal muscle weakness; in adults, it can be associated with malignancy.

Psoriasis vulgaris (plaque type).description: A chronic immune-mediated skin disease with well-demarcated erythematous plaques and silvery scale, often on extensor surfaces; may involve nails with pitting or onycholysis.

Allergic/irritant contact dermatitis (ha.description: Inflammatory dermatitis due to contact allergens or irritants; presents with erythema, scaling, fissuring, and pruritus on hands, often related to exposures.

Tinea manuum.description: Dermatophyte infection of the hand presenting with annular scaly plaques or diffuse hyperkeratosis; often unilateral and associated with tinea pedis.

Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE).description: A physeal disorder of the proximal femur in adolescents in which the femoral head (epiphysis) slips posteroinferiorly relative to the neck, often requiring in-situ pinning.

Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease (avascular ne.normalized_text: Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease (avascular necrosis of the femoral head in childhood)
Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease (avascular ne.description: Idiopathic avascular necrosis of the capital femoral epiphysis in children leading to fragmentation, collapse, and remodeling of the femoral head.

Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH).description: A spectrum of abnormalities in which the acetabulum and femoral head are maldeveloped, leading to subluxation or dislocation, commonly identified in infancy or early childhood.

Proximal femoral physeal fracture (Salte.normalized_text: Proximal femoral physeal fracture (Salter-Harris I of the proximal femur)
Proximal femoral physeal fracture (Salte.description: An acute traumatic separation through the proximal femoral growth plate that can mimic SCFE radiographically, often associated with acute pain and inability to bear weight.

Gastric outlet obstruction (mechanical,.description: Blockage at or near the pylorus/duodenal bulb that prevents gastric emptying, leading to marked stomach dilation and a large intragastric air–fluid level.

Pyloric channel scarring from peptic ulc.normalized_text: Pyloric channel scarring from peptic ulcer disease (cause of gastric outlet obstruction)
Pyloric channel scarring from peptic ulc.description: Chronic peptic ulcer disease can cause inflammation and fibrosis of the pyloric channel, narrowing the outlet and causing gastric retention.

Gastric volvulus.description: Twisting of the stomach along its axes (organoaxial or mesenteroaxial), which can acutely obstruct the gastroesophageal junction and/or pylorus, causing massive gastric distension and an air–fluid level.

Superior mesenteric artery (SMA) syndrom.description: Compression of the third portion of the duodenum between the SMA and aorta leads to proximal duodenal and gastric dilation and delayed gastric emptying.

Duodenal obstruction from pancreatic hea.normalized_text: Duodenal obstruction from pancreatic head mass (e.g., pancreatic adenocarcinoma)
Duodenal obstruction from pancreatic hea.description: A mass in the pancreatic head can externally compress the duodenum, causing gastric outlet obstruction and gastric dilation.

Krabbe disease (globoid cell leukodystro.description: A lysosomal storage disorder caused by GALC deficiency leading to severe, symmetric demyelination that often involves the periventricular white matter, corticospinal tracts, posterior fossa, and the optic nerves/chiasm; typically presents in infancy but later-onset forms exist.

Metachromatic leukodystrophy.description: An arylsulfatase A deficiency causing progressive demyelination with symmetric periventricular white matter changes that can show a tigroid pattern; classically spares subcortical U-fibers early and may involve corticospinal tracts.

X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (childhood.description: A peroxisomal disorder with accumulation of very long-chain fatty acids causing inflammatory demyelination, classically beginning in the parieto-occipital periventricular white matter and splenium of the corpus callosum.

Multiple sclerosis.description: An immune-mediated demyelinating disease characterized by disseminated CNS lesions, often periventricular (Dawson’s fingers), involving the optic nerves and brainstem/cerebellum; usually relapsing-remitting in young adults but can occur in pediatric patients.

Periventricular leukomalacia (chronic hy.normalized_text: Periventricular leukomalacia (chronic hypoxic-ischemic white matter injury)
Periventricular leukomalacia (chronic hy.description: White matter injury of prematurity or early infancy due to hypoxia-ischemia, leading to periventricular gliosis and volume loss that can appear hyperintense on T2 with ventricular enlargement from parenchymal loss.

diagnoses.name: Primary yolk sac tumor of intestine
diagnoses.normalized_text: Primary yolk sac tumor of intestine
diagnoses.icd11_title: Yolk sac tumour, unspecified site, female

Hepatoid/enteroblastic adenocarcinoma of.normalized_text: Hepatoid/enteroblastic adenocarcinoma of the small intestine (AFP-producing)
Hepatoid/enteroblastic adenocarcinoma of.description: A rare adenocarcinoma with hepatocellular or fetal enteroblastic differentiation that can arise in the gastrointestinal tract and often produces AFP and expresses GPC3; morphology is glandular/solid and epithelial markers are retained, with frequent CDX2 expression.

Primary small bowel adenocarcinoma (conv.description: Malignant epithelial tumor arising from the small intestine, most commonly ileum/jejunum; typically shows glandular differentiation and intestinal markers like CDX2; CK7 and CK20 are variable.

Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma to.normalized_text: Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma to the small bowel
Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma to.description: Secondary involvement of the small intestine by a colorectal primary, often via direct extension or metastasis; typically CDX2 and SATB2 positive and variably CK20 positive, usually CK7 negative.

Metastatic hepatocellular carcinoma invo.normalized_text: Metastatic hepatocellular carcinoma involving the small intestine
Metastatic hepatocellular carcinoma invo.description: Spread of primary liver hepatocellular carcinoma to the gastrointestinal tract; tumors often express AFP and GPC3 and are keratin positive but typically lack intestinal transcription factors like CDX2.

Metastatic yolk sac tumor (germ cell tum.normalized_text: Metastatic yolk sac tumor (germ cell tumor) to the small intestine
Metastatic yolk sac tumor (germ cell tum.description: A germ cell tumor that can rarely metastasize to GI tract; typically shows AFP and GPC3 positivity with germ cell markers such as SALL4 and sometimes OCT4.

Meckel's diverticulum with ectopic gastr.normalized_text: Meckel's diverticulum with ectopic gastric mucosa (bleeding Meckel)
Meckel's diverticulum with ectopic gastr.description: A congenital ileal diverticulum that may contain ectopic gastric mucosa, leading to acid-induced ulceration and painless lower gastrointestinal bleeding; classically detected by Tc-99m pertechnetate scan showing a focus in the right lower quadrant that appears with and parallels gastric activity.

Small-bowel angiodysplasia (vascular mal.normalized_text: Small-bowel angiodysplasia (vascular malformation) with active bleeding
Small-bowel angiodysplasia (vascular mal.description: Degenerative vascular malformations of the gastrointestinal tract that can cause intermittent or chronic bleeding, often identified on tagged red blood cell scans when bleeding is active.

Peptic ulcer disease with upper gastroin.normalized_text: Peptic ulcer disease with upper gastrointestinal bleeding
Peptic ulcer disease with upper gastroin.description: Erosions or ulcers in the stomach or duodenum that can bleed and cause acute or chronic iron-deficiency anemia; bleeding may be detected on nuclear scans if active.

Crohn disease with gastrointestinal blee.normalized_text: Crohn disease with gastrointestinal bleeding and protein-losing enteropathy
Crohn disease with gastrointestinal blee.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease affecting any part of the GI tract, which can cause mucosal ulceration, bleeding, systemic inflammation, and protein loss.

Small-intestinal tumor (e.g., gastrointe.normalized_text: Small-intestinal tumor (e.g., gastrointestinal stromal tumor) with bleeding
Small-intestinal tumor (e.g., gastrointe.description: Neoplasms of the small intestine, such as GISTs, can ulcerate and bleed, causing iron-deficiency anemia; active bleeding may be localized by tagged RBC scans.

diagnoses.name: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia
diagnoses.normalized_text: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia
diagnoses.icd11_title: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia

Rounded atelectasis (folded lung).description: A pleural-based, round or wedge-shaped area of atelectasis that forms adjacent to pleural disease (effusion or thickening); vessels and bronchi curve toward the lesion (comet-tail sign).

Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis.description: A hypersensitivity reaction to airway colonization by Aspergillus leading to asthma exacerbations, central bronchiectasis, and high-attenuation mucoid impaction.

Endobronchial tumor (e.g., carcinoid or.normalized_text: Endobronchial tumor (e.g., carcinoid or obstructing neoplasm) with post-obstructive changes
Endobronchial tumor (e.g., carcinoid or.description: A focal endobronchial lesion can obstruct a lobar/segmental bronchus causing distal mucus impaction, atelectasis, and recurrent infection.

Constrictive bronchiolitis (bronchioliti.normalized_text: Constrictive bronchiolitis (bronchiolitis obliterans) / small airways disease
Constrictive bronchiolitis (bronchioliti.description: Inflammatory and fibrotic narrowing of small airways causing air-trapping and mosaic attenuation, often more evident on expiratory CT.

Pleural pseudotumor (loculated pleural e.normalized_text: Pleural pseudotumor (loculated pleural effusion in a fissure)
Pleural pseudotumor (loculated pleural e.description: A lenticular, mass-like collection of fluid trapped within a pleural fissure, often associated with heart failure or pleuritis; can mimic a tumor.

Post-primary (reactivation) pulmonary tu.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection with reactivation in adults or older children, characteristically involving the apical/posterior segments of the upper lobes and forming cavitary necrotizing granulomas.

Necrotizing bacterial pneumonia with lun.normalized_text: Necrotizing bacterial pneumonia with lung abscess (e.g., Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella, anaerobic aspiration)
Necrotizing bacterial pneumonia with lun.description: Severe bacterial infection causing tissue necrosis and cavitation; may follow aspiration or hematogenous spread and can produce air–fluid–level cavities (abscesses).

Pulmonary nocardiosis.description: Opportunistic infection by Nocardia species causing cavitary consolidations and nodules, often in immunocompromised hosts and mimicking TB or fungal disease.

Chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis.description: A chronic fungal infection by Aspergillus spp. in structurally abnormal lungs, leading to slowly progressive upper-lobe cavities that may contain fungal balls.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegene.description: ANCA-associated necrotizing vasculitis causing cavitating pulmonary nodules/masses, upper airway disease, and renal involvement.

Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopat.description: Opportunistic demyelinating disease of the CNS caused by JC polyomavirus reactivation in immunosuppressed patients (commonly advanced HIV).

JC virus granule cell neuronopathy (JCV.normalized_text: JC virus granule cell neuronopathy (JCV GCN)
JC virus granule cell neuronopathy (JCV.description: Infection of cerebellar granule cells by JC virus causing progressive cerebellar ataxia; occurs in severe immunosuppression, including HIV.

Primary central nervous system lymphoma.normalized_text: Primary central nervous system lymphoma (PCNSL, AIDS-related)
Primary central nervous system lymphoma.description: EBV-driven diffuse large B-cell lymphoma arising in the CNS in severely immunocompromised patients, including those with advanced HIV.

Toxoplasma gondii encephalitis.description: Reactivation of latent Toxoplasma in the brain of immunocompromised patients, causing focal neurologic deficits and ring-enhancing lesions.

Cryptococcal meningitis.description: Fungal meningitis due to Cryptococcus neoformans in advanced HIV, often with elevated opening pressure and subacute meningoencephalitis.

Fabry disease (alpha-galactosidase A def.description: X‑linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficient alpha‑galactosidase A leading to globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) accumulation in vascular endothelium, kidneys, and heart; presents with proteinuric kidney disease and concentric LV hypertrophy with conduction abnormalities.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM).description: Genetic cardiomyopathy characterized by unexplained LV hypertrophy, often asymmetric, with myocyte disarray and potential for arrhythmias and sudden death.

Cardiac amyloidosis.description: Systemic deposition of misfolded amyloid fibrils (AL or ATTR) in myocardium and other organs causing restrictive cardiomyopathy and often nephrotic-range proteinuria.

Danon disease (LAMP2 deficiency).description: X‑linked vacuolar myopathy with cardiomyopathy due to lysosomal-associated membrane protein-2 deficiency; frequently presents with severe LV hypertrophy and pre-excitation on ECG.

PRKAG2 syndrome (glycogen storage cardio.normalized_text: PRKAG2 syndrome (glycogen storage cardiomyopathy with pre-excitation)
PRKAG2 syndrome (glycogen storage cardio.description: Autosomal dominant disorder of cardiac AMP-activated protein kinase leading to glycogen accumulation, ventricular hypertrophy, and accessory pathway-mediated pre-excitation.

Pericardial effusion (possible cardiac t.description: Accumulation of excess fluid in the pericardial sac; when large or rapidly accumulating, it can impair cardiac filling and cause tamponade.

Dilated cardiomyopathy.description: A myocardial disease characterized by ventricular dilation and systolic dysfunction, often presenting with heart failure signs.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (including a.description: Genetic cardiomyopathy with asymmetric myocardial hypertrophy; apical variant shows thickening at the apex and can cause diastolic dysfunction and arrhythmias.

Left ventricular thrombus.description: An intracavitary clot typically forming in areas of akinesis/hypokinesis (e.g., post-MI or severe cardiomyopathy), posing risk for systemic embolization.

Right heart enlargement due to pulmonary.normalized_text: Right heart enlargement due to pulmonary hypertension
Right heart enlargement due to pulmonary.description: Elevated pulmonary arterial pressure leads to right ventricular hypertrophy/dilation and possible right heart failure.

Herpes zoster (cranial nerve distributio.normalized_text: Herpes zoster (cranial nerve distribution, trigeminal and possible facial nerve involvement)
Herpes zoster (cranial nerve distributio.description: Reactivation of varicella-zoster virus causing a painful, unilateral vesicular eruption in a dermatomal pattern; in the face it may involve trigeminal branches and can extend to the ear when multiple cranial nerves are involved, particularly in older or immunocompromised patients.

Herpes zoster oticus (Ramsay Hunt syndro.description: Varicella-zoster virus reactivation in the geniculate ganglion of the facial nerve leading to vesicles in the ear canal/pinna and potentially severe ear pain and facial nerve palsy; rash can extend to adjacent facial areas.

Herpes zoster ophthalmicus.description: Reactivation of varicella-zoster virus in the ophthalmic (V1) branch of the trigeminal nerve, producing a unilateral vesicular eruption on the forehead, scalp, and around the eye; can threaten ocular structures.

Impetigo (nonbullous/bullous).description: Superficial bacterial skin infection (usually Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes) characterized by vesicles/pustules that rupture to form honey-colored crusts; bullous form produces larger flaccid bullae.

Pemphigus vulgaris.description: Autoimmune blistering disorder causing fragile intraepidermal (flaccid) bullae and erosions, often starting in the oral mucosa and spreading to the skin; can involve the face and scalp.

Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA).description: Focal dilatation of the abdominal aorta; risk of rupture increases with diameter >5.5 cm. Can occasionally compress adjacent structures.

Obstructive uropathy due to ureteric cal.normalized_text: Obstructive uropathy due to ureteric calculus
Obstructive uropathy due to ureteric cal.description: Blockage of urinary flow by a stone in the ureter causing upstream dilation and hydronephrosis.

Extrinsic ureteral compression from abdo.normalized_text: Extrinsic ureteral compression from abdominal aortic/iliac aneurysm
Extrinsic ureteral compression from abdo.description: Mechanical obstruction of the ureter caused by mass effect from a nearby aneurysm, leading to hydronephrosis without an intraluminal stone.

Ureteral urothelial carcinoma.description: Malignancy of the ureteral epithelium causing luminal narrowing/obstruction and secondary hydronephrosis.

Pelviureteric junction (PUJ) obstruction.description: Functional or anatomical narrowing at the renal pelvis-ureter junction leading to hydronephrosis; can be congenital or acquired.

Gram-negative septic shock with dissemin.normalized_text: Gram-negative septic shock with disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)
Gram-negative septic shock with dissemin.description: Life‑threatening infection by gram‑negative bacilli causing systemic inflammatory response, circulatory failure, and DIC leading to multiorgan dysfunction.

Purpura fulminans (sepsis‑associated).description: Acute, rapidly progressive cutaneous purpura and skin necrosis due to DIC and microvascular thrombosis, most often triggered by severe bacterial sepsis.

Capnocytophaga canimorsus septicemia (do.normalized_text: Capnocytophaga canimorsus septicemia (dog/cat exposure–related) with DIC
Capnocytophaga canimorsus septicemia (do.description: Severe sepsis caused by thin gram‑negative rods from dog or cat oral flora; can rapidly progress to DIC, purpura fulminans, shock liver, and multiorgan failure, especially in asplenic or alcoholic patients.

Thrombotic microangiopathy (atypical hem.description: Complement‑mediated or secondary microvascular thrombosis causing hemolytic anemia with schistocytes, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury.

Ischemic hepatitis (shock liver) seconda.normalized_text: Ischemic hepatitis (shock liver) secondary to septic shock
Ischemic hepatitis (shock liver) seconda.description: Acute hepatocellular injury from hypoperfusion leading to dramatic AST/ALT elevations and transient coagulopathy during shock states.

diagnoses.name: MELAS syndrome
diagnoses.icd11_title: MELAS - [Mitochondrial encephalopathy with lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes] syndrome

Cardioembolic ischemic stroke from left.normalized_text: Cardioembolic ischemic stroke from left ventricular (LV) apical thrombus
Cardioembolic ischemic stroke from left.description: An acute arterial ischemic stroke caused by an embolus originating from an LV apical mural thrombus, often forming after myocardial infarction or severe LV dysfunction.

Ischemic stroke secondary to atrial fibr.normalized_text: Ischemic stroke secondary to atrial fibrillation with left atrial appendage thrombus
Ischemic stroke secondary to atrial fibr.description: Embolic stroke due to thrombus formation in the left atrial appendage from atrial fibrillation, which then embolizes to the cerebral circulation.

Ischemic stroke from infective endocardi.normalized_text: Ischemic stroke from infective endocarditis (septic emboli)
Ischemic stroke from infective endocardi.description: Vegetations on cardiac valves can embolize to cerebral arteries causing acute ischemic strokes, often cortical and large-vessel occlusions.

Ischemic stroke due to left ventricular.normalized_text: Ischemic stroke due to left ventricular aneurysm with mural thrombus (post-myocardial infarction)
Ischemic stroke due to left ventricular.description: Following a transmural myocardial infarction, an LV aneurysm can form with associated mural thrombus that can embolize and cause stroke.

Paradoxical embolic stroke via patent fo.normalized_text: Paradoxical embolic stroke via patent foramen ovale (PFO) with venous thromboembolism
Paradoxical embolic stroke via patent fo.description: A venous thrombus crosses a right-to-left shunt (e.g., PFO) and embolizes to the cerebral circulation, causing an acute ischemic stroke.

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (head o.normalized_text: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (head of pancreas) with obstructive jaundice
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (head o.description: Malignant epithelial tumor of the pancreatic ducts, often arising in the head where it causes extrahepatic biliary obstruction and cholestasis; CA 19-9 is frequently elevated and liver metastases can occur.

Perihilar cholangiocarcinoma (Klatskin t.description: Adenocarcinoma arising from the bile duct epithelium near the hepatic hilum, causing intrahepatic biliary obstruction and cholestasis; frequently presents with jaundice and elevated CA 19-9.

Distal cholangiocarcinoma (extrahepatic.description: Malignancy of the distal common bile duct that often mimics pancreatic head cancer by producing obstructive jaundice and elevated cholestatic enzymes; CA 19-9 may be high.

Gallbladder carcinoma with biliary obstr.description: Adenocarcinoma of the gallbladder that can invade the biliary tree, producing obstructive jaundice and elevated cholestatic enzymes; tumor markers such as CA 19-9 may rise.

IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis/auto.description: Immune-mediated fibroinflammatory disease involving the pancreas and bile ducts, causing strictures and obstructive jaundice; can mimic pancreatic or biliary malignancy on imaging and may respond to steroids.

Choledocholithiasis with obstructive jau.normalized_text: Choledocholithiasis with obstructive jaundice (with or without mild gallstone pancreatitis)
Choledocholithiasis with obstructive jau.description: A gallstone obstructing the common bile duct causes extrahepatic cholestasis; transient pancreatic duct obstruction can mildly elevate lipase; CA 19-9 can rise in benign obstruction but usually normalizes after relief.

Acute calculous cholecystitis.description: Acute inflammation of the gallbladder typically caused by an obstructing gallstone in the cystic duct or neck, leading to gallbladder distension, wall thickening, edema, and possible pericholecystic fluid.

Choledocholithiasis with obstructive jau.description: Stone(s) in the common bile duct causing partial or complete obstruction, potentially leading to jaundice, cholestatic liver enzyme elevation, and complications like cholangitis or pancreatitis.

Mirizzi syndrome.description: Impaction of a gallstone in the cystic duct or Hartmann’s pouch causing extrinsic compression of the common hepatic duct, leading to obstructive jaundice and recurrent inflammation; can progress to cholecystocholedochal fistula.

Gallstone ileus.description: Mechanical small bowel obstruction due to a large gallstone that has passed through a biliary-enteric fistula; often shows ectopic calcified stone, bowel obstruction, and sometimes pneumobilia.

Gallbladder carcinoma.description: Malignancy of the gallbladder, often associated with longstanding gallstones and chronic inflammation; presents with mass replacing gallbladder, wall thickening, or polypoid lesions and can cause biliary obstruction.

Patellar tendon rupture.description: A disruption of the patellar tendon leading to loss of continuity between the patella and tibial tubercle, often causing a high-riding patella (patella alta) and inability to actively extend the knee.

Tibial tubercle avulsion fracture.description: An avulsion of the tibial tubercle apophysis, typically in adolescents, due to forceful quadriceps contraction; can produce patella alta if the patellar tendon remains taut and pulls proximally.

Transient lateral patellar dislocation (.description: Acute lateral displacement of the patella that often spontaneously reduces; commonly in adolescents/young adults and associated with hemarthrosis and characteristic radiographic findings post-reduction.

Osgood–Schlatter disease (tibial tubercl.description: Overuse-related traction apophysitis of the tibial tubercle in adolescents, due to repetitive strain from the patellar tendon, leading to pain and possible prominence/fragmentation at the tubercle.

Eruptive vellus hair cysts (EVHC).description: A benign follicular developmental disorder characterized by numerous small dermal cysts that contain keratin and vellus hairs; lesions present as multiple tiny follicular papules, often brownish, sometimes with a central punctum.

Steatocystoma multiplex.description: A disorder with numerous sebum-filled dermal cysts arising from the pilosebaceous unit; lesions are usually soft, translucent to yellow papules/nodules and may exude oily fluid.

Keratosis pilaris.description: A common keratinization disorder with follicular plugging that produces rough, small keratotic papules on extensor surfaces.

Multiple epidermoid (infundibular) cysts.description: Benign keratin-filled cysts derived from the follicular infundibulum; usually present as firm nodules with a central punctum.

Lichen spinulosus.description: An uncommon follicular disorder with grouped patches of spiny hyperkeratotic follicular papules, often on extensor surfaces in adolescents and young adults.

Cutaneous leishmaniasis (Old World/New W.description: Protozoal infection (Leishmania) transmitted by sandflies that causes chronic papules or nodules that ulcerate with raised indurated borders and heal with atrophic scars; histology shows granulomatous inflammation with parasitized macrophages (amastigotes) early, later pauciparasitic granulomas.

Pyoderma gangrenosum.description: A neutrophilic dermatosis characterized by rapidly progressive, painful ulcers with undermined violaceous borders, often following minor trauma and associated with systemic diseases such as IBD or arthritis.

Buruli ulcer (Mycobacterium ulcerans inf.description: A necrotizing cutaneous infection caused by M. ulcerans, producing painless, undermined ulcers on limbs due to mycolactone toxin; common in tropical regions and heals with scarring.

Sporotrichosis (cutaneous/lymphocutaneou.description: A subcutaneous fungal infection caused by Sporothrix schenckii complex; inoculation leads to nodules that may ulcerate and can spread along lymphatics in a chain.

Ecthyma (deep impetigo due to streptococ.description: A deeper bacterial infection of the epidermis/dermis presenting as punched-out ulcerations with overlying crusts on the lower legs; can heal with scars.

diagnoses.name: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor
diagnoses.icd11_title: Gastrointestinal stromal tumour of unspecified gastrointestinal sites

Monophasic synovial sarcoma.description: A malignant soft tissue sarcoma often composed of uniform spindle cells; characteristically expresses epithelial markers (cytokeratin, EMA) and TLE1, and is associated with the t(X;18)(p11;q11) SS18::SSX fusion.

Ewing sarcoma / Primitive neuroectoderma.description: A small round blue cell tumor of bone and soft tissue, typically showing diffuse membranous CD99 and NKX2.2 positivity and EWSR1 gene rearrangements.

Epithelioid sarcoma (including proximal-.description: A malignant soft tissue tumor characterized by epithelioid and sometimes rhabdoid cells; commonly expresses cytokeratin and EMA, often CD34, with loss of INI1/SMARCB1.

Rhabdomyosarcoma (alveolar/embryonal).description: A malignant skeletal muscle tumor of children and young adults; shows small round blue cells and myogenic marker positivity (myogenin, MyoD1, desmin).

Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor.description: An aggressive spindle cell sarcoma arising from peripheral nerves; may show S100/SOX10 in a subset and often displays high cellularity and mitotic activity.

diagnoses.name: Malignant gastrointestinal stromal tumor
diagnoses.icd11_title: Malignant GIST - [gastrointestinal stromal tumour] of large intestine

Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm (SPN) of.normalized_text: Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm (SPN) of the pancreas
Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm (SPN) of.description: A rare, low-grade malignant pancreatic tumor, typically in young women, characterized by a well-encapsulated solid-cystic mass with hemorrhage and pseudopapillary architecture; immunophenotype often vimentin+, CD10/PR+, nuclear beta-catenin, and usually negative or weak for chromogranin.

Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor (pNET).description: Neoplasms arising from pancreatic neuroendocrine cells; often well-circumscribed and hypervascular, may be functional or nonfunctional, with solid nests/trabeculae on histology and strong neuroendocrine markers.

Acinar cell carcinoma of the pancreas.normalized_text: Acinar cell carcinoma of the pancreas
Acinar cell carcinoma of the pancreas.description: A malignant pancreatic exocrine tumor derived from acinar cells; often large and well-circumscribed with solid sheets and may show necrosis; expresses digestive enzymes (trypsin, chymotrypsin, BCL10).

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.description: The most common pancreatic malignancy; typically ill-defined, infiltrative, desmoplastic mass causing ductal obstruction and often lacks a well-formed capsule.

Extragastrointestinal gastrointestinal s.normalized_text: Extragastrointestinal gastrointestinal stromal tumor (EGIST) adjacent to pancreas
Extragastrointestinal gastrointestinal s.description: A rare mesenchymal tumor similar to GIST but arising outside the GI tract (e.g., retroperitoneum/pancreatic vicinity); typically spindle/epithelioid cells, often c-KIT/DOG1 positive, and may be well-circumscribed with hemorrhage.

Multiple epidermolytic acanthomas (inter.description: Benign clonal epidermal proliferations showing epidermolytic hyperkeratosis on histology. They present as multiple skin-colored to brown, verrucous papules that often cluster and coalesce in intertriginous sites such as the axillae and neck.

Acanthosis nigricans.description: Velvety hyperpigmented thickening of intertriginous skin, commonly associated with insulin resistance or internal malignancy in select cases.

Confluent and reticulated papillomatosis.description: Disorder of keratinization characterized by hyperpigmented, slightly verrucous papules and plaques that become confluent centrally and reticulated peripherally, classically on the central chest and upper back, sometimes neck.

Seborrheic keratoses (multiple, flexural.description: Common benign epidermal tumors presenting as 'stuck-on,' verrucous, hyperkeratotic papules or plaques; can be pigmented and occur in large numbers in older adults.

Darier disease (keratosis follicularis).description: Autosomal dominant keratinization disorder with greasy, hyperkeratotic papules in seborrheic and flexural areas; histology shows acantholysis and dyskeratosis (corps ronds and grains).

Aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC).description: Benign, expansile, blood-filled cystic lesion of bone that can be primary or occur secondarily within another tumor; common in adolescents and young adults and can present with multiloculated, septated cavities and fluid–fluid levels.

Giant cell tumor of bone (GCT) with seco.normalized_text: Giant cell tumor of bone (GCT) with secondary ABC change
Giant cell tumor of bone (GCT) with seco.description: Locally aggressive benign tumor of osteoclast-like giant cells, typically in skeletally mature patients; can undergo secondary aneurysmal change producing fluid–fluid levels.

Telangiectatic osteosarcoma.description: High-grade malignant osteosarcoma variant composed of blood-filled spaces that can mimic ABC radiologically but shows malignant solid components and produces osteoid.

Chondromyxoid fibroma (often with second.normalized_text: Chondromyxoid fibroma (often with secondary ABC-like change)
Chondromyxoid fibroma (often with second.description: Rare benign cartilage-derived tumor characterized by lobulated chondromyxoid tissue; usually metaphyseal in long bones but can occur in the pelvis and may show internal septations and occasional cystic change.

Solitary plasmacytoma of bone.description: Localized proliferation of monoclonal plasma cells, most often in axial skeleton; presents as a lytic lesion and is typically FDG-avid, sometimes preceding multiple myeloma.

Stiff-person syndrome (classic, anti-GAD.description: Autoimmune disorder characterized by fluctuating axial and proximal limb stiffness and stimulus-triggered spasms; commonly associated with high-titer anti-GAD antibodies and continuous motor unit activity on EMG.

Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigid.normalized_text: Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus (PERM)
Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigid.description: A severe form within the stiff-person spectrum featuring diffuse rigidity, myoclonus, brainstem involvement, autonomic dysfunction, and encephalopathy; often associated with glycine receptor antibodies.

Acquired neuromyotonia (Isaac's syndrome.description: Peripheral nerve hyperexcitability disorder causing continuous muscle fiber activity, cramps, fasciculations, and stiffness; often autoimmune (VGKC-complex antibodies).

Tetanus.description: Acute neurotoxin-mediated disorder causing generalized rigidity and painful spasms due to disinhibition of motor neurons.

Paraneoplastic stiff-person spectrum dis.description: Stiff-person phenotype associated with malignancy (often breast or small-cell lung) and antibodies such as anti-amphiphysin; may include focal stiff-limb syndrome.

Takayasu arteritis.description: A chronic, granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis primarily affecting the aorta and its major branches, leading to stenosis, occlusion, or aneurysm; most common in younger women.

Giant cell arteritis (temporal arteritis.description: An immune-mediated granulomatous vasculitis of medium and large arteries in adults, often involving the extracranial branches of the carotid, causing ischemic complications.

Atherosclerotic carotid artery disease w.normalized_text: Atherosclerotic carotid artery disease with external carotid ischemia
Atherosclerotic carotid artery disease w.description: Atherosclerotic narrowing of the carotid arteries can reduce perfusion to the scalp via external carotid branches, rarely causing ischemic scalp ulcers in severe disease.

Polyarteritis nodosa.description: A necrotizing vasculitis of medium-sized arteries causing ischemia and infarction in multiple organs; cutaneous manifestations include ulcers and nodules.

Infectious necrotic ulcer (e.g., ecthyma.normalized_text: Infectious necrotic ulcer (e.g., ecthyma gangrenosum or necrotizing soft tissue infection)
Infectious necrotic ulcer (e.g., ecthyma.description: Rapidly progressive necrotic skin lesions due to invasive bacterial infection (often Pseudomonas) leading to black eschar and ulceration, typically in immunocompromised hosts.

Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar).description: A parasitic infection caused by Leishmania donovani complex, characterized by reticuloendothelial system involvement with amastigotes (Leishman-Donovan bodies) in macrophages; typically presents with prolonged fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia, and hypergammaglobulinemia.

Disseminated histoplasmosis.description: A systemic fungal infection due to Histoplasma capsulatum, often in immunocompromised hosts; organisms are small yeasts that can be found within macrophages in bone marrow, causing fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias, and sometimes cholestatic or hepatic dysfunction.
