Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH).description: A hyperinflammatory syndrome driven by uncontrolled immune activation, often triggered by infections (including Leishmania), malignancy, or autoimmune disease; presents with persistent fever, splenomegaly, cytopenias, hyperferritinemia, liver dysfunction, and can cause jaundice.

Necrobiosis lipoidica.description: A chronic granulomatous disorder often on the shins, characterized by collagen degeneration, lipid deposition, and atrophic yellow-brown plaques with erythematous borders; associated with diabetes in many patients.

Granuloma annulare.description: A benign inflammatory dermatosis presenting as annular plaques or papules, most often on distal extremities; histology shows palisading granulomas with mucin.

Tinea corporis (dermatophyte infection).description: A superficial fungal infection of glabrous skin causing annular, scaly plaques with an advancing border and central clearing.

Erythema migrans (early Lyme disease).description: The early cutaneous manifestation of Borrelia burgdorferi infection, presenting as an expanding annular erythematous lesion at a tick bite site, sometimes with central clearing.

Nummular (discoid) dermatitis.description: An eczematous condition causing coin-shaped pruritic plaques, commonly on the legs, with erythema and scaling.

Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1B (GNAS i.description: End-organ resistance to parathyroid hormone due to abnormal methylation at the GNAS locus (often at NESP/AS/XL/A/B). Characterized by hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, elevated PTH, usually normal renal function, and may show resistance to other hormones such as TSH.

Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A (GNAS i.normalized_text: Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A (GNAS inactivating mutation with Albright hereditary osteodystrophy)
Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A (GNAS i.description: PTH resistance due to inactivating mutations in the GNAS gene, typically accompanied by Albright hereditary osteodystrophy (AHO) features and multihormone resistance (including TSH).

Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 2.description: PTH resistance with impaired signaling downstream of cAMP generation; biochemically similar to other PHP types (hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, elevated PTH) but typically without GNAS methylation defects.

Hypoparathyroidism (autoimmune or postsu.description: Deficient PTH secretion leads to hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia; can be autoimmune, genetic, or postsurgical.

Acute phosphate load–induced hypocalcemi.normalized_text: Acute phosphate load–induced hypocalcemia (e.g., phosphate enema use, tumor lysis, rhabdomyolysis)
Acute phosphate load–induced hypocalcemi.description: A sudden rise in serum phosphate can complex with calcium, lowering serum calcium and stimulating PTH despite normal renal function.

Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH).description: A hyperinflammatory syndrome caused by uncontrolled immune activation (often triggered by infection, malignancy, or autoimmune disease) leading to cytokine storm, cytopenias, liver dysfunction, coagulopathy, and multiorgan failure.

Sepsis with disseminated intravascular c.description: Systemic infection can trigger widespread coagulation activation leading to consumption of platelets and coagulation factors, microvascular thrombosis, bleeding risk, and multiorgan dysfunction.

Leptospirosis (Weil disease).description: A spirochetal zoonosis that can cause a biphasic illness with jaundice, renal failure, myositis (elevated CK), hemorrhagic manifestations, and DIC.

COVID-19 (acute SARS-CoV-2 infection) wi.normalized_text: COVID-19 (acute SARS-CoV-2 infection) with multiorgan involvement
COVID-19 (acute SARS-CoV-2 infection) wi.description: SARS-CoV-2 can cause severe disease with lymphopenia, coagulopathy (elevated D-dimer), hepatic injury, kidney injury, and diverse lung imaging findings.

Thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) such as.description: Disorders characterized by microvascular thrombosis causing thrombocytopenia, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, and organ injury (classically kidney and brain).

Disseminated histoplasmosis (or other di.normalized_text: Disseminated histoplasmosis (or other disseminated fungal infection)
Disseminated histoplasmosis (or other di.description: Opportunistic fungal infection that can disseminate to the reticuloendothelial system causing fever, hepatosplenic involvement, cytopenias, coagulopathy, and pulmonary nodules/ground-glass opacities.

Ovarian clear cell carcinoma (OCCC).description: An epithelial ovarian cancer subtype characterized by clear cytoplasm, hobnail cells, and frequent association with endometriosis; typically shows immunopositivity for HNF-1β and Napsin A and ER-negativity.

Endometrioma (ovarian endometriosis) wit.description: Benign cystic lesion of the ovary composed of endometrial glands and stroma; may present as a "chocolate cyst" on imaging and is a known precursor/association for clear cell carcinoma.

Metastatic clear cell renal cell carcino.normalized_text: Metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma (RCC) to the ovary
Metastatic clear cell renal cell carcino.description: Metastatic spread of RCC can rarely involve the ovary; shows clear cells but usually has an RCC immunophenotype (PAX8 variable, RCC marker, CD10 positive) and typically lacks HNF-1β-driven profile.

Syringomyelia secondary to Chiari I malf.normalized_text: Syringomyelia secondary to Chiari I malformation
Syringomyelia secondary to Chiari I malf.description: A fluid-filled cavity (syrinx) within the spinal cord caused by impaired cerebrospinal fluid flow at the foramen magnum due to tonsillar ectopia. Can be familial and may present in adolescence or adulthood with progressive sensory loss and weakness.

Intramedullary spinal cord ependymoma wi.normalized_text: Intramedullary spinal cord ependymoma with associated syringomyelia
Intramedullary spinal cord ependymoma wi.description: Ependymomas are intramedullary tumors that often form centrally and can be associated with a rostral or caudal syrinx due to altered CSF flow. Typically present in cervical or thoracic cord in adults.

Primary (idiopathic) syringomyelia / hyd.description: A congenital or developmental dilatation of the central canal (hydromyelia) or formation of a syrinx without an identifiable associated lesion such as Chiari, tumor, or trauma.

Post-traumatic syringomyelia.description: Formation of a syrinx months to years after spinal cord injury due to scarring and altered CSF dynamics, leading to progressive myelopathy and neuropathic pain.

Cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA) with p.normalized_text: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA) with possible CAA-related inflammation
Cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA) with p.description: Deposition of beta-amyloid in cortical/leptomeningeal vessels causing lobar microbleeds, cortical superficial siderosis, and sometimes asymmetric inflammatory edema (CAA-ri) with subacute neurologic deficits.

Acute cortical ischemic stroke.description: Focal arterial occlusion causing cytotoxic edema with diffusion restriction and evolving FLAIR hyperintensity in a cortical territory.

Peri-ictal changes from recent seizure/s.normalized_text: Peri-ictal changes from recent seizure/status epilepticus
Peri-ictal changes from recent seizure/s.description: Seizure activity can cause transient cortical diffusion restriction and FLAIR hyperintensity due to metabolic demand and cytotoxic/vasogenic changes.

Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (CJD).description: Rapidly progressive prion disease that often shows cortical ribboning and basal ganglia diffusion restriction with rapidly progressive dementia and myoclonus.

Posterior reversible encephalopathy synd.description: Reversible vasogenic edema, typically in posterior regions, associated with hypertension, cytotoxic agents, or eclampsia; may show FLAIR hyperintensity and occasionally microhemorrhages.

Neurosarcoidosis (spinal cord sarcoidosi.description: Granulomatous inflammatory disease due to sarcoidosis involving the central nervous system; can cause intramedullary spinal cord lesions and leptomeningeal enhancement.

Tuberculous granuloma (spinal tuberculom.description: Mycobacterial infection of the spine or spinal cord causing caseating granulomas and intramedullary lesions; may mimic sarcoidosis or tumors on MRI.

Fungal granulomatous myelitis (e.g., his.description: Fungal infection of the spinal cord or meninges producing granulomatous inflammation and enhancing lesions, often in immunocompromised hosts.

Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (.normalized_text: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (AQP4-IgG) with longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis
Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (.description: Autoimmune astrocytopathy characterized by severe, often longitudinally extensive spinal cord inflammation; can present with cervical cord lesions.

Intramedullary neoplasm (e.g., astrocyto.description: Primary spinal cord tumors that often present as enhancing intramedullary masses with cord expansion.

Lung abscess (bacterial).description: A localized area of suppurative necrosis of lung tissue leading to a cavitary lesion, usually due to aspiration or severe bacterial pneumonia.

Necrotizing pneumonia.description: A severe form of bacterial pneumonia (e.g., Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella, anaerobes) characterized by parenchymal necrosis and multiple small cavities that may coalesce.

Post-primary pulmonary tuberculosis (cav.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection in previously sensitized individuals, often causing cavitary disease due to caseating necrosis.

Cavitating squamous cell carcinoma of th.normalized_text: Cavitating squamous cell carcinoma of the lung
Cavitating squamous cell carcinoma of th.description: A primary lung malignancy (often central) prone to central necrosis and cavitation, presenting as a thick-walled cavitary mass.

Septic pulmonary emboli with cavitary no.normalized_text: Septic pulmonary emboli with cavitary nodules
Septic pulmonary emboli with cavitary no.description: Hematogenous spread of infected thrombi (e.g., from right-sided endocarditis or infected catheters) causing multiple peripheral nodules that can cavitate.

Cysticercosis (Taenia solium larval cyst.description: Tissue infection by the larval stage (cysticercus) of Taenia solium. The cyst typically has a three-layered wall and contains an invaginated scolex with suckers/hooklets; calcareous corpuscles may be present in the parenchyma.

Hydatid disease (Echinococcus granulosus.description: Infection with larval hydatid cysts characterized by a thick acellular laminated membrane and an inner germinal layer that produces brood capsules and numerous protoscolices (hydatid sand); daughter cysts may be present.

Coenurosis (Taenia multiceps larval infe.description: Tissue infection with coenurus larvae of Taenia species, where a single cyst contains multiple scolices attached to the inner wall, often in neural or subcutaneous tissues.

Sparganosis (Spirometra spp. plerocercoi.description: Infection with plerocercoid larvae (spargana) of Spirometra tapeworms, presenting as elongated, ribbon-like larvae within subcutaneous tissues or organs, often with chronic inflammation and fibrosis.

Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP, Ric.description: A neurodegenerative tauopathy characterized by vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, axial rigidity, early postural instability, and characteristic midbrain atrophy on MRI (hummingbird/penguin sign).

Parkinson's disease.description: A synucleinopathy causing bradykinesia, rigidity, resting tremor, and postural instability, often with hypomimia; eye movements are usually preserved early.

Multiple system atrophy (MSA).description: A neurodegenerative synucleinopathy with parkinsonian and/or cerebellar features and prominent autonomic failure; imaging may show pontine and cerebellar changes (e.g., hot-cross-bun sign).

Chronic progressive external ophthalmopl.normalized_text: Chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia (CPEO)/Oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy (OPMD)
Chronic progressive external ophthalmopl.description: Mitochondrial myopathy (CPEO) or late-onset muscular dystrophy (OPMD) causing bilateral ptosis and progressive external ophthalmoplegia, often with dysphagia in OPMD.

Cryptococcal meningoencephalitis (Crypto.description: Opportunistic fungal infection of the central nervous system caused by encapsulated yeast. Typically presents with subacute meningitis/meningoencephalitis and elevated intracranial pressure. India ink of CSF shows round budding yeasts with prominent polysaccharide capsules; brain tissue may show "soap-bubble" lesions.

Coccidioidal meningitis (Coccidioides im.description: Disseminated coccidioidomycosis can involve the meninges, causing chronic basilar meningitis with high relapse risk. CSF may show spherules containing endospores, and diagnosis is supported by serology/culture.

Candida meningitis.description: Rare fungal meningitis usually in neurosurgical patients, neonates, or the immunocompromised. Candida appears as budding yeasts (sometimes with pseudohyphae) in CSF; diagnosis confirmed by culture or PCR.

Central nervous system histoplasmosis.description: Disseminated Histoplasma capsulatum infection can involve the CNS, leading to chronic meningitis or focal lesions. Yeasts are small and often intracellular; diagnosis relies on antigen testing, PCR, culture, or pathology.

Acute pontine ischemic stroke (paramedia.normalized_text: Acute pontine ischemic stroke (paramedian pontine infarct)
Acute pontine ischemic stroke (paramedia.description: An infarction of the pons due to occlusion of perforating branches of the basilar artery, often presenting with acute brainstem signs and diffusion restriction on MRI.

Central pontine myelinolysis (osmotic de.description: A demyelinating disorder of the central pons typically following rapid correction of hyponatremia or severe electrolyte shifts, producing symmetric T2 hyperintensity in the pons.

Listeria rhombencephalitis.description: Brainstem encephalitis caused by Listeria monocytogenes, often affecting the pons and medulla, with MRI showing T2 hyperintensity and possible diffusion restriction in the brainstem.

Multiple sclerosis (brainstem plaque).description: An immune-mediated demyelinating disease producing focal plaques in the central nervous system; brainstem involvement can appear as T2 hyperintense lesions in the pons.

Diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma / diffu.normalized_text: Diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma / diffuse midline glioma (adult)
Diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma / diffu.description: An infiltrative glioma of the pons characterized by T2 hyperintensity and pontine enlargement; although more common in children, can occur in adults.

Babesiosis.description: Intraerythrocytic protozoal infection (Babesia species) transmitted by ticks or transfusion; causes hemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia. Smear can show multiple ring forms per RBC and characteristic tetrads (Maltese cross).

Severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria.description: Life-threatening malaria with high parasitemia; shows multiple delicate ring forms per RBC and can cause hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, elevated LDH/AST, and coagulopathy.

Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP.description: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia due to ADAMTS13 deficiency leading to platelet-rich thrombi; presents with hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, and elevated LDH, sometimes with neurologic changes.

Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS).description: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with thrombocytopenia, often triggered by Shiga-toxin; classically involves acute kidney injury and elevated LDH.

Disseminated intravascular coagulation (.normalized_text: Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) secondary to severe infection
Disseminated intravascular coagulation (.description: Systemic activation of coagulation causing consumption of platelets and clotting factors; leads to elevated D-dimer, thrombocytopenia, and anemia from hemolysis.

Uterine leiomyosarcoma with pulmonary an.normalized_text: Uterine leiomyosarcoma with pulmonary and hepatic metastases
Uterine leiomyosarcoma with pulmonary an.description: An aggressive malignant tumor arising from uterine smooth muscle that often presents with a pelvic mass and can spread hematogenously to lungs and liver.

Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (cho.normalized_text: Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (choriocarcinoma) with lung metastases
Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (cho.description: A malignant trophoblastic tumor that arises after pregnancy events and commonly metastasizes hematogenously to the lungs and sometimes liver.

Benign metastasizing leiomyoma (BML).description: A rare condition where histologically benign uterine leiomyomas are associated with slow-growing extrauterine nodules, most commonly in the lungs, usually in women with current or prior uterine fibroids or after hysterectomy.

Epithelial ovarian carcinoma with metast.description: A malignant ovarian tumor that often presents with a pelvic mass and can spread transcoelomically and hematogenously to the liver and, less commonly, to the lungs.

Disseminated granulomatous infection (e..normalized_text: Disseminated granulomatous infection (e.g., tuberculosis or histoplasmosis)
Disseminated granulomatous infection (e..description: Systemic infections that can cause multiple pulmonary nodules and hepatic lesions; pelvic calcifications could be incidental fibroid.

Graves disease with thyrotoxic periodic.normalized_text: Graves disease with thyrotoxic periodic paralysis (TPP)
Graves disease with thyrotoxic periodic.description: Autoimmune hyperthyroidism causing diffuse thyroid hypervascularity and hyperfunction. In susceptible patients (often men of Asian ancestry), hyperthyroidism can precipitate TPP, characterized by profound intracellular potassium shift and severe hypokalemia, sometimes with muscle weakness and hypercapnic respiratory acidosis.

Toxic multinodular goiter with thyrotoxi.normalized_text: Toxic multinodular goiter with thyrotoxicosis-induced periodic paralysis
Toxic multinodular goiter with thyrotoxi.description: Autonomously functioning thyroid nodules produce excess thyroid hormone, leading to thyrotoxicosis that can trigger hypokalemic periodic paralysis.

Hashitoxicosis (transient thyrotoxicosis.description: Early or fluctuating phase of autoimmune (Hashimoto) thyroiditis where hormone leakage causes transient thyrotoxicosis; in rare cases this can precipitate hypokalemic periodic paralysis.

Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrom.description: Autonomous aldosterone secretion leads to renal potassium wasting and hypertension; classically causes metabolic alkalosis and mild hyperglycemia.

Bifid uvula (anatomic variant).description: A congenital split or cleft of the uvula that is usually benign and asymptomatic; may occur in isolation or be associated with submucous cleft palate.

Submucous cleft palate.description: A congenital defect where the muscles of the soft palate are cleft under intact mucosa; often associated with a bifid uvula and can cause velopharyngeal insufficiency.

Uvular papilloma.description: A benign squamous papilloma, often HPV-associated, presenting as a pedunculated or lobulated exophytic lesion on the uvula.

Uvular hypertrophy.description: Enlargement of the uvula that can be idiopathic or related to chronic irritation, snoring, or obstructive sleep apnea.

Uvulitis (infectious or allergic).description: Inflammation and swelling of the uvula due to infection, allergy, trauma, or irritants; can cause sore throat and airway symptoms.

diagnoses.name: Intervertebral disc prolapse
diagnoses.icd11_title: Intervertebral disc degeneration without prolapsed disc with determinant

Lumbar disc herniation.description: Focal protrusion or extrusion of intervertebral disc material that can compress adjacent nerve roots, causing back pain and radicular symptoms.

Lumbar spinal stenosis.description: Narrowing of the spinal canal and/or neural foramina, often due to degenerative changes, leading to compression of neural elements and possible neurogenic claudication.

Degenerative disc disease (lumbar spondy.description: Age-related degeneration of intervertebral discs and adjacent vertebral structures, which can cause chronic low back pain and contribute to disc height loss and osteophyte formation.

Degenerative spondylolisthesis.description: Anterior slippage of a vertebral body due to facet joint and disc degeneration, potentially causing nerve root compression and back/leg symptoms.

Cauda equina syndrome (secondary to seve.normalized_text: Cauda equina syndrome (secondary to severe lumbar stenosis or large disc herniation)
Cauda equina syndrome (secondary to seve.description: Compression of the cauda equina nerve roots, typically from a large central disc herniation or severe stenosis; presents with back pain, bilateral leg symptoms, saddle anesthesia, and bowel/bladder dysfunction; a surgical emergency.

Infective endocarditis with septic embol.normalized_text: Infective endocarditis with septic emboli and intracranial mycotic aneurysms
Infective endocarditis with septic embol.description: Bacterial infection of cardiac valves causing showering of septic emboli to the brain and lungs; may form distal (mycotic) cerebral aneurysms and septic pulmonary emboli.

Septic pulmonary emboli from right-sided.normalized_text: Septic pulmonary emboli from right-sided endocarditis (e.g., tricuspid) with secondary brain emboli
Septic pulmonary emboli from right-sided.description: Right-sided valvular infection (often in IV drug use) leading to embolization of infected thrombi to lungs and occasionally paradoxical/systemic emboli causing brain infarcts/abscesses.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegene.normalized_text: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener) with pulmonary nodules and CNS vasculitis
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegene.description: ANCA-associated small to medium vessel vasculitis causing necrotizing granulomas in the respiratory tract and kidneys; can cause cavitary lung nodules and CNS ischemia/aneurysms due to vasculitis.

Primary angiitis of the central nervous.normalized_text: Primary angiitis of the central nervous system (PACNS)
Primary angiitis of the central nervous.description: Idiopathic vasculitis confined to the CNS causing multifocal ischemia and aneurysmal changes without systemic involvement.

Disseminated fungal infection (e.g., inv.normalized_text: Disseminated fungal infection (e.g., invasive aspergillosis) with pulmonary nodules and CNS involvement
Disseminated fungal infection (e.g., inv.description: Angioinvasive fungal disease starting in lungs and spreading hematogenously to the brain, producing infarcts, hemorrhagic lesions, or mycotic aneurysms.

Hodgkin lymphoma.description: A malignant lymphoproliferative disease characterized by FDG-avid lymphadenopathy, often involving mediastinal nodes; can generate a hypercoagulable state and provoke venous thromboembolism.

Sarcoidosis.description: A multisystem granulomatous disease characterized by noncaseating granulomas and symmetric FDG-avid hilar/mediastinal lymphadenopathy; can involve liver and other organs.

Tuberculosis (intrathoracic lymph node T.description: Mycobacterial infection causing caseating granulomatous inflammation with FDG-avid lymph nodes; may present with mediastinal/hilar lymphadenopathy and can lead to hypercoagulability and PE.

Metastatic solid malignancy with cancer-.normalized_text: Metastatic solid malignancy with cancer-associated thrombosis
Metastatic solid malignancy with cancer-.description: Disseminated malignancy (e.g., lung, GI, or unknown primary) with nodal metastases that are FDG-avid and a propensity to cause venous thromboembolism.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA).description: ANCA-associated necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis that affects the respiratory tract and can be FDG-avid; vasculitis can predispose to thrombosis and pulmonary emboli.

Autosomal dominant osteopetrosis (Albers.description: A genetic disorder of impaired osteoclast-mediated bone resorption leading to abnormally dense but brittle bones and narrowed marrow spaces. Adult forms often present with diffuse osteosclerosis, high BMD, and characteristic radiographic changes.

Paget disease of bone (sclerotic phase).description: A focal disorder of accelerated bone remodeling with excessive resorption followed by disorganized formation; later stages show dense, enlarged, sclerotic bone.

Sclerostin pathway disorders (sclerosteo.normalized_text: Sclerostin pathway disorders (sclerosteosis/van Buchem disease) or LRP5 high bone mass
Sclerostin pathway disorders (sclerosteo.description: Inherited high bone mass syndromes due to reduced sclerostin activity or activating LRP5 mutations, causing increased osteoblast activity and markedly elevated BMD.

Skeletal fluorosis.description: Chronic excessive fluoride exposure leads to increased bone formation, osteosclerosis, and ligament/tendon calcifications; often presents with high BMD and dense bones on imaging.

Diffuse osteoblastic metastases (e.g., p.description: Metastatic spread from osteoblastic tumors can cause widespread osteosclerosis, particularly in the axial skeleton and pelvis, elevating measured BMD.

Autoimmune lymphocytic hypophysitis (inf.description: Immune-mediated inflammation of the pituitary and stalk that can involve the anterior and posterior pituitary, leading to hypopituitarism, hyperprolactinemia (stalk effect), and central diabetes insipidus; MRI often shows stalk thickening/enhancing sellar–suprasellar lesion; CSF may show mild inflammatory changes.

Neurosarcoidosis involving the hypothala.description: Granulomatous inflammation from sarcoidosis that can infiltrate the pituitary, stalk, and hypothalamus causing panhypopituitarism and central diabetes insipidus; MRI may show enhancing lesions and stalk thickening; CSF often shows inflammatory changes with elevated protein and pleocytosis.

Craniopharyngioma (suprasellar mass).description: Epithelial tumor of the sellar/suprasellar region that commonly causes compression of the optic chiasm and hypothalamic–pituitary dysfunction; can lead to hypopituitarism and diabetes insipidus, often seen on MRI as a suprasellar mass.

Pituitary macroadenoma with stalk effect.description: A benign pituitary tumor >1 cm that can compress the optic chiasm and impair pituitary function; stalk compression can raise prolactin; anterior hypopituitarism is common.

Suprasellar germinoma.description: A CNS germ cell tumor that often arises in the suprasellar region, frequently causing central diabetes insipidus and hypopituitarism in younger patients; may show an enhancing stalk/hypothalamic mass.

Atrial myxoma (left atrial).description: A benign cardiac tumor most often arising from the interatrial septum in the left atrium, typically pedunculated and mobile, which can prolapse through the mitral valve and cause obstructive or embolic symptoms.

Left atrial thrombus (often in setting o.normalized_text: Left atrial thrombus (often in setting of atrial fibrillation or atrial enlargement)
Left atrial thrombus (often in setting o.description: An intracardiac clot, most commonly forming in the left atrial appendage, associated with stasis (e.g., atrial fibrillation) and risk of systemic embolization.

Infective endocarditis with mitral valve.normalized_text: Infective endocarditis with mitral valve vegetation
Infective endocarditis with mitral valve.description: Infection of the endocardial surface leading to friable vegetations on valves; can cause regurgitation, emboli, and systemic signs of infection.

Second-degree atrioventricular block, Mo.normalized_text: Second-degree atrioventricular block, Mobitz type I (Wenckebach)
Second-degree atrioventricular block, Mo.description: Progressive prolongation of the PR interval culminating in a nonconducted P wave, resulting in grouped beating; often due to AV nodal conduction delay.

Premature atrial contractions (PACs).description: Early atrial depolarizations originating outside the sinus node, producing early P waves with different morphology and a noncompensatory pause; commonly benign but can cause palpitations or trigger other arrhythmias.

Infantile-onset Pompe disease (Glycogen.normalized_text: Infantile-onset Pompe disease (Glycogen storage disease type II)
Infantile-onset Pompe disease (Glycogen.description: Autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by acid alpha-glucosidase (GAA) deficiency leading to glycogen accumulation, especially in cardiac and skeletal muscle; presents in infancy with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and progressive weakness.

Danon disease (LAMP2 deficiency).description: X-linked dominant lysosomal/autophagic disorder due to LAMP2 deficiency, causing early hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, skeletal myopathy, and sometimes cognitive issues.

Primary systemic carnitine deficiency.description: Autosomal recessive defect in carnitine transporter (SLC22A5) leading to impaired fatty acid oxidation; can present in infancy with cardiomyopathy and hypoketotic hypoglycemia.

Glycogen storage disease type III (Cori/.normalized_text: Glycogen storage disease type III (Cori/Forbes disease)
Glycogen storage disease type III (Cori/.description: Autosomal recessive debranching enzyme (AGL) deficiency causing glycogen accumulation in liver and muscle; can lead to hepatomegaly and cardiomyopathy in some patients.

Mitochondrial cardiomyopathy.description: Cardiomyopathy due to defects in mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation; may present in infancy with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and multi-system features.

Linfoma B-linfoblástico/leucemia linfobl.description: Una neoplasia maligna de células B precursoras que puede presentarse con afectación de la médula ósea (LLA) y/o masas extranodales de tejido blando (LBL). Frecuentemente asociada con LDH elevada y marcadores inflamatorios sistémicos; La PET/TC suele mostrar lesiones intensamente hipermetabólicas.

Anemia de enfermedad crónica/inflamación.description: Anemia hipoproliferativa provocada por citocinas inflamatorias que causan secuestro de hierro y eritropoiesis deteriorada. Típicamente normocítica o ligeramente microcítica y acompañada de ferritina elevada y marcadores inflamatorios.

Anemia por deficiencia de hierro.description: Anemia por hierro insuficiente que lleva a una reducción de la síntesis de hemoglobina; clásicamente microcítica e hipocrómica.

Anemia hemolítica autoinmune (AIHA).description: Destrucción mediada por el sistema inmunitario de glóbulos rojos que conduce a anemia con LDH elevado, bilirrubina indirecta y reticulocitosis.

Piomiositis/abscesos profundos de tejido.description: Infección bacteriana del músculo esquelético que causa abscesos focales; se presenta con dolor/hinchazón localizada, inflamación sistémica y puede mostrar masas ávidas de FDG en PET/TC.

Linfoma no Hodgkin (por ejemplo, linfoma.normalized_text: Linfoma no Hodgkin (por ejemplo, linfoma difuso de células B grandes) con afectación extranodal
Linfoma no Hodgkin (por ejemplo, linfoma.description: Linfoma agresivo de células B que puede afectar ganglios y sitios extranodales, produciendo masas ávidas por FDG y LDH elevado; la anemia puede deberse a una enfermedad crónica o a la afectación de la médula.

Cellulitis (gluteal).description: An acute bacterial infection of the skin and subcutaneous tissue, most often due to streptococci or Staphylococcus aureus, causing diffuse inflammation.

Cutaneous abscess (gluteal).description: A focal collection of pus within the dermis or subcutaneous tissue, commonly caused by S. aureus, often presenting with a tender, fluctuant nodule.

Necrotizing soft tissue infection.description: A rapidly progressive, life-threatening infection of fascia and subcutaneous tissue characterized by severe pain, systemic toxicity, and tissue necrosis.

Hidradenitis suppurativa (HS).description: A chronic inflammatory disorder of hair follicles in intertriginous areas leading to recurrent nodules, abscesses, and sinus tracts.

Irritant or allergic contact dermatitis.normalized_text: Irritant or allergic contact dermatitis (intertriginous area)
Irritant or allergic contact dermatitis.description: Inflammation of the skin from contact with an irritant or allergen, often causing erythema, edema, and pruritus, especially in moist, friction-prone areas.

Dermatomyositis.description: An autoimmune inflammatory myopathy characterized by proximal muscle weakness and distinctive cutaneous findings including heliotrope rash and Gottron papules; can be amyopathic with skin-only disease.

Subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (.description: A photosensitive autoimmune cutaneous lupus presenting with annular or papulosquamous lesions on sun-exposed areas; often spares knuckles and may be associated with anti-Ro/SSA antibodies.

Rosacea.description: A chronic inflammatory facial dermatosis with centrofacial erythema, flushing, telangiectasias, and possible papules/pustules; typically limited to the face.

Seborrheic dermatitis.description: Inflammatory skin condition affecting sebaceous areas (scalp, face, chest) with erythema and greasy scale; often chronic and relapsing.

Photoallergic or phototoxic drug eruptio.description: A cutaneous reaction triggered by medication and sunlight exposure, presenting with erythema and dermatitis in sun-exposed areas; may resemble eczema or lupus-like rashes.

Multiple/eruptive keratoacanthomas (KA).description: Benign but rapidly growing crateriform tumors derived from hair follicle epithelium; single or multiple lesions may erupt on sun‑exposed skin and can show Koebnerization. Histology overlaps with well‑differentiated cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma.

Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC).description: Malignant proliferation of keratinocytes often arising on sun‑exposed skin; can present as rapidly enlarging hyperkeratotic nodules or ulcers and may resemble keratoacanthoma histologically.

Hypertrophic actinic keratosis.description: A premalignant lesion due to chronic ultraviolet exposure; presents as hyperkeratotic, scaly papules or plaques that can become thick and crusted and may progress to SCC.

Verruca vulgaris (common warts).description: Benign HPV-induced papillomas that present as hyperkeratotic, verrucous papules; may Koebnerize at sites of trauma.

Bowen disease (squamous cell carcinoma i.normalized_text: Bowen disease (squamous cell carcinoma in situ)
Bowen disease (squamous cell carcinoma i.description: Intraepidermal SCC presenting as slowly enlarging erythematous, scaly plaques; can progress to invasive SCC without treatment.

Pyoderma gangrenosum.description: A neutrophilic dermatosis causing painful, rapidly progressive ulcers with undermined violaceous borders; lesions show pathergy and may be associated with systemic disease.

Dorsal arachnoid web.description: A thin intradural arachnoid membrane in the dorsal thoracic spine that focally indents the cord, producing the classic ‘scalpel sign’ (sharp anterior displacement/kinking of the cord) and myelopathic symptoms.

Dorsal spinal arachnoid cyst (intradural.description: A CSF-filled arachnoid-lined sac in the dorsal thoracic canal that can compress and anteriorly displace the spinal cord, causing myelopathy.

Ventral spinal cord herniation.description: Anterior displacement of the spinal cord through a ventral dural defect, most often in the mid-thoracic region, leading to focal kinking and myelopathy.

Ossified or hypertrophied ligamentum fla.normalized_text: Ossified or hypertrophied ligamentum flavum (posterior epidural compression)
Ossified or hypertrophied ligamentum fla.description: Degenerative thickening or ossification of the ligamentum flavum in the thoracic spine causing posterior epidural mass effect and cord compression.

Intradural extramedullary tumor (e.g., d.normalized_text: Intradural extramedullary tumor (e.g., dorsal thoracic meningioma)
Intradural extramedullary tumor (e.g., d.description: A dural-based tumor, commonly meningioma in the thoracic spine, that compresses the spinal cord from the dorsal or dorsolateral aspect.

T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymp.description: A malignant proliferation of immature T-lymphoblasts that typically presents with circulating blasts and bone marrow involvement; often associated with rearrangements of the T-cell receptor loci (e.g., 14q11 TCRAD).

B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-A.description: A malignancy of immature B-lymphoblasts that presents with bone marrow failure and circulating blasts; characterized by B-lineage markers and various cytogenetic abnormalities.

Acute myeloid leukemia (AML).description: A clonal proliferation of myeloid blasts leading to bone marrow failure and circulating blasts; often shows myeloid-specific morphology and cytogenetic features.

Mixed phenotype acute leukemia (MPAL).description: An acute leukemia expressing antigens of more than one lineage (e.g., myeloid and lymphoid), often with complex cytogenetics.

T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia (T-PLL).description: An aggressive mature T-cell leukemia of adults, frequently associated with rearrangements of chromosome 14 (TCR loci) or X; presents with very high lymphocytosis, splenomegaly, and mature T-cell morphology.

Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH).description: A life‑threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome caused by uncontrolled activation of macrophages and T cells, leading to cytokine storm, multiorgan dysfunction, and cytopenias.

Sepsis with disseminated intravascular c.description: Systemic infection causing dysregulated host response and consumptive coagulopathy, often presenting with thrombocytopenia, low fibrinogen, anemia, and organ injury including lungs.

Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL, a sub.normalized_text: Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL, a subtype of AML)
Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL, a sub.description: An acute leukemia characterized by promyelocytes and a high risk of DIC; patients often present with cytopenias and coagulopathy.

Severe COVID-19 pneumonia with hyperinfl.normalized_text: Severe COVID-19 pneumonia with hyperinflammatory syndrome
Severe COVID-19 pneumonia with hyperinfl.description: SARS-CoV-2 infection can cause diffuse viral pneumonia and a cytokine storm with high ferritin and coagulopathy.

Miliary/disseminated tuberculosis with s.description: Disseminated Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection can trigger HLH, presenting with severe systemic inflammation, cytopenias, and lung infiltrates.

Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (superi.normalized_text: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (superior sagittal sinus)
Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (superi.description: Thrombosis of a dural venous sinus leading to impaired venous drainage, venous congestion, and venous infarction/hemorrhage; commonly involves the superior sagittal sinus and can cause multifocal cortical lesions and diffusion restriction.

Embolic ischemic stroke (arterial, e.g.,.description: Acute arterial occlusions from emboli cause abrupt ischemia with diffusion-restricted cortical infarcts, often in multiple territories when embolic.

Central nervous system vasculitis.description: Inflammation of cerebral vessels leading to multifocal ischemia; can present with scattered cortical-subcortical lesions on MRI.

Septic emboli with cerebral microabscess.description: Hematogenous spread of infection (e.g., endocarditis) can seed the brain, producing multiple diffusion-restricting lesions and, over time, ring-enhancing abscesses.

Posterior reversible encephalopathy synd.description: Reversible vasogenic edema often in parieto-occipital regions due to blood pressure dysregulation or endothelial injury; can show FLAIR hyperintensities and occasionally restricted diffusion.

IgA vasculitis (Henoch–Schönlein purpura.description: Immune complex–mediated small-vessel vasculitis characterized by IgA deposition in postcapillary venules, typically causing palpable purpura on the lower extremities, arthralgias, abdominal pain, and possible renal involvement; more common in children but occurs in adults.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegene.description: ANCA-associated small- to medium-vessel vasculitis with granulomatous inflammation, commonly involving the upper airways (chronic sinusitis, crusting, septal perforation), lungs, and kidneys; skin purpura can occur.

Levamisole-adulterated cocaine–associate.description: Immune complex and ANCA-associated vasculitis triggered by exposure to levamisole-adulterated cocaine; presents with retiform or palpable purpura, often on ears and legs, necrosis of nasal septum, and can show neutropenia.

Cryoglobulinemic vasculitis.description: Immune complex–mediated small-vessel vasculitis due to circulating cryoglobulins (often associated with hepatitis C, autoimmune disease, or lymphoproliferative disorders), causing palpable purpura, arthralgias, neuropathy, and possible renal disease.

Idiopathic/drug-induced cutaneous leukoc.description: Hypersensitivity-mediated small-vessel vasculitis limited to the skin, often triggered by infections or medications; presents with palpable purpura predominantly on dependent areas and may resolve with removal of trigger.

Oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (l.normalized_text: Oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (likely tonsillar) with metastatic cervical lymphadenopathy
Oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (l.description: Malignancy of the oropharyngeal mucosa (often tonsil/base of tongue), frequently HPV-associated, that commonly presents with a primary mucosal lesion and ipsilateral level II–III nodal metastases, which may be cystic/necrotic and FDG-avid.

Metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma w.normalized_text: Metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma with cervical nodal metastasis
Metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma w.description: Differentiated thyroid cancer (papillary type) often metastasizes to cervical lymph nodes, which can appear cystic and may be PET-avid; microcalcifications and a thyroid primary nodule are typical.

Lymphoma (Hodgkin or non-Hodgkin) involv.normalized_text: Lymphoma (Hodgkin or non-Hodgkin) involving cervical lymph nodes
Lymphoma (Hodgkin or non-Hodgkin) involv.description: Malignancy of lymphoid tissue that often presents with enlarged FDG-avid lymph nodes; cervical nodes are commonly involved.

Second branchial cleft cyst (with possib.normalized_text: Second branchial cleft cyst (with possible superinfection)
Second branchial cleft cyst (with possib.description: A congenital cystic lesion located along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle (level II region); can present as a cystic neck mass and may become inflamed or infected.

Tuberculous cervical lymphadenitis (scro.description: Mycobacterial infection of cervical lymph nodes causing granulomatous inflammation with caseation, often producing necrotic/cystic nodes; nodes can be FDG-avid.

Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (botryoid var.normalized_text: Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (botryoid variant) of the bladder
Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (botryoid var.description: A pediatric soft-tissue sarcoma arising from skeletal muscle lineage, the botryoid subtype classically presents as a grape-like polypoid mass in hollow viscera such as the bladder and shows a hypercellular subepithelial cambium layer.

Alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma of the bladder.description: A more aggressive rhabdomyosarcoma subtype characterized by PAX3/7–FOXO1 translocations; rare in the bladder but can present as a small round blue cell tumor.

Ewing sarcoma/PNET of the bladder.description: A malignant small round blue cell tumor often harboring EWSR1 rearrangements (e.g., EWSR1-FLI1); primary bladder involvement is rare but reported.

Small cell neuroendocrine carcinoma of t.normalized_text: Small cell neuroendocrine carcinoma of the bladder
Small cell neuroendocrine carcinoma of t.description: An aggressive neuroendocrine carcinoma composed of small round blue cells, usually arising from urothelial epithelium; more common in older adults.

Primary or secondary lymphoma involving.normalized_text: Primary or secondary lymphoma involving the bladder
Primary or secondary lymphoma involving.description: Lymphoid neoplasms can rarely present in the bladder as masses; histology shows sheets of lymphoid cells.

Bladder (vesical) calculus.description: A stone formed in the urinary bladder, often due to urinary stasis, obstruction, infection, or foreign bodies; classically appears as a round or ovoid, laminated, radiopaque mass centered over the pelvis on plain radiograph.

Calcified uterine fibroid (leiomyoma).description: Benign smooth muscle tumor of the uterus that can undergo dystrophic 'popcorn' or peripheral calcification, seen as coarse, irregular calcifications in the pelvis, often in women of reproductive or perimenopausal age.

Calcified ovarian dermoid (mature cystic.description: A common benign ovarian tumor that can contain fat, teeth, bone, and show calcifications; on radiographs, may present as a pelvic calcified mass with tooth-like or irregular calcific densities.

Bladder tumor with dystrophic calcificat.description: Urothelial carcinoma or other bladder neoplasm that develops irregular dystrophic calcifications within or on the tumor; may appear as a calcified mass projecting over the bladder.

Acute patellar tendon rupture.description: Tear of the patellar tendon leading to loss of continuity between the patella and tibial tubercle. The quadriceps pulls the patella proximally, producing a high-riding patella (patella alta) and loss of active knee extension.

Superior dislocation of the patella.description: A rare condition in which the patella displaces superiorly and may lock over femoral osteophytes, typically in older patients with osteoarthritis.

Chronic patella alta due to patellar ten.normalized_text: Chronic patella alta due to patellar tendon elongation (e.g., prior Osgood-Schlatter disease, previous surgery, or chronic tendinopathy)
Chronic patella alta due to patellar ten.description: Chronic lengthening or laxity of the patellar tendon results in a persistently high-riding patella without acute rupture, often associated with prior apophyseal disease, repetitive overuse, or postoperative changes.

Lateral patellar dislocation (reduced or.normalized_text: Lateral patellar dislocation (reduced or occult on current view)
Lateral patellar dislocation (reduced or.description: Transient lateral displacement of the patella, often in younger individuals, which can spontaneously reduce. Radiographs may be normal except for indirect signs; dedicated axial or AP views are more revealing.

diagnoses.name: Primary pancreatic T-cell/histiocyte-rich large B-cell lymphoma
diagnoses.normalized_text: Primary pancreatic T-cell/histiocyte-rich large B-cell lymphoma

Metastatic high-grade neuroendocrine car.normalized_text: Metastatic high-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma (small-cell type) to the liver
Metastatic high-grade neuroendocrine car.description: An aggressive neuroendocrine malignancy, often arising from lung or gastrointestinal tract, that commonly metastasizes to the liver and shows neuroendocrine marker positivity with a very high proliferative index.

Primary hepatic or secondary involvement.normalized_text: Primary hepatic or secondary involvement by diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
Primary hepatic or secondary involvement.description: A high-grade lymphoma that can present as hepatic masses or diffuse liver involvement; histology shows sheets of atypical lymphoid cells and high proliferation.

Poorly differentiated hepatocellular car.description: A primary liver cancer that in poorly differentiated forms can appear as sheets of atypical cells with high proliferation; usually expresses hepatocellular markers and often arises in a background of chronic liver disease.

Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma to.normalized_text: Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma to the liver
Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma to.description: Colorectal cancer frequently metastasizes to the liver and typically shows glandular structures and colorectal immunophenotype.

Metastatic Ewing sarcoma/primitive neuro.description: A small round blue cell sarcoma that can rarely metastasize to the liver; shows diffuse sheets of small round cells and high proliferation, often with neuroectodermal features.

Osteochondroma (exostosis) of the iliac.description: A benign cartilage-capped bony outgrowth arising from the cortex of bone, often pedunculated and continuous with the host cortex and medullary canal. Commonly presents as a painless, firm mass.

Myositis ossificans (heterotopic ossific.normalized_text: Myositis ossificans (heterotopic ossification) of the hip region
Myositis ossificans (heterotopic ossific.description: Benign, reactive ossification within soft tissues, typically following trauma; shows a zonal pattern of maturation from the periphery inward.

Parosteal osteosarcoma.description: A low-grade surface osteosarcoma arising from the outer periosteal surface, often presenting as a densely ossified, lobulated mass attached to bone.

Extraskeletal osteosarcoma.description: A rare malignant soft tissue tumor that produces osteoid without direct attachment to bone.

Calcified lipoma / osteolipoma.description: A benign lipomatous tumor that contains areas of calcification or ossification, usually arising in soft tissues and presenting as a painless mass.

Lateral tibial plateau fracture (Schatzk.normalized_text: Lateral tibial plateau fracture (Schatzker II: split-depression)
Lateral tibial plateau fracture (Schatzk.description: An intra‑articular fracture of the lateral tibial plateau characterized by a vertical split with depression of the articular surface, typically from a valgus/axial load injury.

Pure depression fracture of the lateral.normalized_text: Pure depression fracture of the lateral tibial plateau (Schatzker III)
Pure depression fracture of the lateral.description: Impaction injury causing depression of the lateral tibial plateau articular surface without a large split component; often from axial load with valgus stress.

Osteoarthritis of the knee.description: Chronic degenerative joint disease characterized by cartilage loss, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis, and joint space narrowing, leading to mechanical knee pain.

Intercondylar eminence (tibial spine) fr.description: Avulsion of the tibial insertion of the anterior cruciate ligament, often from hyperextension or pivoting injury; common in adolescents but can occur in adults.

diagnoses.name: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor
diagnoses.icd11_title: Gastrointestinal stromal tumour of unspecified gastrointestinal sites

Gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST).description: Mesenchymal tumor of the gastrointestinal tract derived from interstitial cells of Cajal; most are KIT or PDGFRA driven and show KIT (CD117) and/or DOG1 positivity.

Gastric leiomyoma/leiomyosarcoma (smooth.description: Benign (leiomyoma) or malignant (leiomyosarcoma) smooth muscle tumors that can occur in the stomach and present as spindle-cell masses.

Gastric schwannoma.description: Benign nerve sheath tumor of the stomach characterized by S100 positivity and spindle cells with peripheral lymphoid cuffs.

Desmoid-type fibromatosis (mesenteric/ab.description: Locally aggressive myofibroblastic proliferation that can involve the mesentery or abdominal wall and mimic GI spindle tumors; usually shows nuclear beta-catenin mutations/positivity.

Solitary fibrous tumor (SFT).description: Mesenchymal tumor characterized by NAB2-STAT6 fusion and STAT6 nuclear positivity; can rarely present in the abdomen and mimic other spindle-cell tumors.

SHORT syndrome.description: A rare autosomal-dominant disorder (often due to PIK3R1 variants) characterized by short stature, partial lipodystrophy, characteristic triangular face with prominent forehead and deep-set eyes, delayed teething, and insulin resistance.

Russell-Silver syndrome.description: An imprinting/epigenetic growth disorder causing severe pre- and postnatal growth restriction, relative macrocephaly, and triangular face; development is often normal or mildly delayed.

Mandibuloacral dysplasia (progeroid lipo.description: A laminopathy (LMNA or ZMPSTE24 variants) with mandibular and clavicular hypoplasia, acro-osteolysis, partial lipodystrophy, progeroid appearance, short stature, and metabolic complications including insulin resistance.

Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome.description: A classic progeroid laminopathy with severe postnatal growth failure, lipodystrophy, thin skin with prominent veins, characteristic facies, and progressive vascular disease; intellect is typically normal.

Congenital generalized lipodystrophy (Be.description: A rare autosomal-recessive disorder with near-total absence of adipose tissue from birth, muscular appearance, hepatomegaly, and early severe insulin resistance; facial dysmorphism is usually mild.
